t.gast roudkhan@37.1,49.2:
Gilan, on the Caspian side of the Alborz mountains in northern Iran, is a different world from the dry plateau most people imagine when they think of the country. It is green, damp and densely forested, with rice paddies on the coastal plain and tea gardens on the slopes. Rudkhan Castle stands in the forested hills south-west of Fuman, high on a ridge above a river valley, and it is one of the region's best loved historic sites.

The castle is a brick and stone fortress that follows the contours of two peaks, with walls and towers snaking through the trees. It is generally attributed to the Seljuk era or earlier, with later rebuilding, and its local nickname refers to its many steps: the climb up from the parking area through the forest takes a good half-hour or more, on stone stairs beside a rushing stream. Bring decent footwear, because the path is often wet. At the top, the views over the forested valleys are lovely, especially when mist hangs in the trees.

Riding in Iran is a serious undertaking. Visa and entry rules are complex, foreign motorcycle travellers usually need a carnet de passage for their own bike, and the political situation can change quickly. Check your own government's travel advice before planning anything. On the road, traffic is chaotic by European standards and you should ride defensively. That said, the roads of Gilan are scenic: the route from Fuman toward the hill village of Masuleh, with its houses stacked so that the roof of one forms the street of the next, climbs into the mountains through forest and is spectacular. Fog and rain are common, so expect slippery surfaces.

Fuman, about twenty-three kilometres away, has fuel and is known throughout Iran for its kolucheh, a small round cookie filled with walnut paste. Gilan's cuisine is distinctive, with lots of herbs, garlic, sour pomegranate and fish from the Caspian. Rasht, the provincial capital, is the main city for services. Spring and early summer are the best times to visit, when the forest is at its greenest.
t.siahroud e roudbar@36.9,49.7:
The Sefid Rud, the white river, is the great river of northern Iran, cutting a gorge through the Alborz mountains on its way from the plateau to the Caspian Sea. Where it breaks through, around the towns of Manjil and Rudbar in Gilan province, the landscape changes in a matter of kilometres from dry, windswept hills to the dense, humid forests of the Caspian slope. Siahroud, in the Rudbar district, lies in this transitional zone, about thirty kilometres from Manjil.

The Rudbar area is known to archaeologists for its ancient cemeteries. The most famous, Marlik, excavated in the early 1960s, yielded gold and silver vessels, bronze figures and pottery from the late second and early first millennium BC, now among the treasures of the National Museum in Tehran. Other sites in the valleys of the district have revealed burials, kilns and settlements of the same period, suggesting a wealthy culture that controlled the routes between the plateau and the Caspian. Expect excavated ground rather than a visitor attraction.

The region is also known for olives. The valley of the Sefid Rud around Rudbar is one of the few places in Iran where olive trees grow, and the roadside stalls sell olives, olive oil and a local paste made with walnuts and pomegranate. Manjil is known for its wind: the gorge funnels strong winds, and it was the site of one of Iran's first wind farms, with turbines lining the hills. In 1990, a devastating earthquake struck the Manjil-Rudbar area, killing tens of thousands of people, and its memory remains strong.

The main road from Qazvin to Rasht follows the Sefid Rud gorge and is a busy highway with heavy truck traffic, though the views are dramatic. Side roads into the mountain villages are narrower and rougher. Riding in Iran requires careful preparation: entry rules for foreign vehicles, fuel arrangements and the political situation all need checking, as does your government's travel advice. Traffic is chaotic, so ride defensively.

Manjil, Rudbar and Rasht have fuel and food. Spring and autumn are the best times to visit, when the hills are green and the weather mild.
t.sheikh safi al din khanegah and shrine e:
Ardabil is a cold, high city on a plateau beneath the volcanic bulk of Mount Sabalan, and at its heart, a few steps from busy streets, lies the shrine of Sheikh Safi al-Din. He was a Sufi master who died in 1334, and his order grew so powerful that his descendants founded a dynasty: in 1501 Shah Ismail I, of Safi's line, made himself ruler of Iran and established the Safavids, who turned Shia Islam into the state religion. Ismail is buried here too, and the whole ensemble, with its tombs, prayer halls, courtyards and kitchens, became a World Heritage Site in 2010.

The building that makes people gasp is the Chini Khaneh, the china house, a hall whose walls are honeycombed with hundreds of niches shaped to hold individual pieces of porcelain. Shah Abbas I donated a great collection of Chinese ceramics to the shrine, and much of it later went to museums elsewhere, but the empty, gilded niches are almost more beautiful without it. The shrine also gave its name to the Ardabil Carpet, one of the most famous Persian carpets in the world, woven in the sixteenth century and now in London. Wander slowly; the tile work, calligraphy and painted ceilings reward patience.

Ardabil sits at around 1,350 metres, so even in summer the evenings are cool and winters are properly cold, with snow. The region is famous for honey from the meadows of Sabalan, for hot springs at Sarein, a short ride west, and for hearty food built for that climate: thick soups, kebabs and sweet halva. Locals are mostly Azeri speakers, and the welcome is warm.

For a rider the jewel of the area is the road east to Astara on the Caspian, over the Heyran pass. It climbs through open upland and then plunges through dense Hyrcanian forest in a long series of bends, with mist hanging in the trees and the Azerbaijan border close by. Traffic can be heavy on holidays, and fog and rain on the Caspian side make the surface greasy, so take it easy. Westwards, the roads around Sabalan offer high, empty country with snow on the summit well into summer.

Ardabil is a big city with plentiful fuel, workshops and food. As elsewhere in Iran, foreign riders need a carnet and should check current visa and travel conditions before setting out.
t.istisuchay valley@38.5,48.7:
In the far southeast of Azerbaijan, where the Talysh mountains rise from the Caspian lowlands near the border with Iran, the İstisuchay valley winds into a world of dense, damp forest. The name means hot water river, and the valley is known for its thermal springs, which locals have used for bathing and healing for generations. The forests here are Hyrcanian, a relic of the ancient broadleaf woodland that once covered much of the region before the Ice Ages, with ironwood, chestnut-leaved oak and hornbeam, and they have been added to the UNESCO listing of the Hyrcanian Forests. In spring and autumn, mist drifts through the trees, and the green is intense.

The Talysh people, who speak an Iranian language related to Persian, live in the villages of the mountains and lowlands, and their culture has its own songs, dress and cooking. The lowlands around Lankaran and Astara are famous for tea plantations, citrus orchards and rice paddies, a subtropical landscape unlike anything else in the Caucasus. Lankaran cuisine is celebrated across Azerbaijan, especially lavangi, chicken or fish stuffed with walnuts, onions and sour plum paste and baked in a clay oven.

The riding is a mix of good main roads and rough mountain tracks. The highway along the Caspian coast from Baku to Astara is fast and straight, with heavy traffic and plenty of police. Turning into the mountains, the roads become narrower and more interesting, climbing through forest along river valleys with tight bends and steep gradients. Surfaces deteriorate quickly, with potholes, gravel and mud after rain, which is frequent; this is the wettest region of Azerbaijan. Cows, sheep and dogs share the road.

Astara, on the Azerbaijani side of the border, is the nearest town with fuel and shops, and there is a busy border crossing to the Iranian town of the same name. Lankaran, a little further north, is larger and has more choice. Kizhaba and the mountain villages have small shops and teahouses where you will be offered tea in a pear-shaped glass, with jam or a sugar cube.

Check the travel advice before you go, particularly for border areas, and be aware that riding in Azerbaijan requires an international driving permit and that police checks are frequent. Spring, when the forests are at their freshest, and autumn, when the leaves turn, are the best seasons.
t.engelhardt astronomical observatory@55.8:
There is a good story behind this observatory, and it involves a retired astronomer's generosity. Vasily Engelhardt, a Russian nobleman who spent decades observing the sky from his private observatory in Dresden, gave his instruments to Kazan University in the late 1890s, and the university built a new observatory for them on a hill outside the city. It is a quiet, wooded site, far from the lights of Kazan, with domes and small buildings set among trees. For a motorcyclist it is an unusual sort of sight, a place devoted to looking up.

The setting is the Volga country of Tatarstan, a land of rolling fields, birch woods and slow, wide water. A few kilometres away the Volga has been dammed into a long reservoir, and the hill country on the right bank rises steeply above it. Sviyazhsk, the island town founded by Ivan the Terrible in the sixteenth century as a staging post for the conquest of Kazan, lies nearby, and its Assumption Cathedral and Monastery appear on the same ride. Tatarstan itself is an interesting mix of Tatar and Russian culture, and you will see mosques and Orthodox churches in the same villages.

Roads in the area are straightforward. The federal highway between Kazan and Moscow runs close by, wide and fast, with heavy lorry traffic, and the smaller roads that lead to the observatory are quiet and usually in decent condition. Corners are gentle, gradients modest, and there are long straights where you must watch for speed cameras and slow tractors. Summer is warm and sometimes humid, and the best times are late May and September, when the woods are fresh or turning. Winter is long and cold, and the roads can be icy from November.

Vasil'yevo, about six kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafés, so fill up there before you head out. If you want a meal, try chak-chak, the sticky honey sweet that Tatar families serve with tea, or echpochmak, a triangular pastry of meat and potato. Visiting the observatory itself may require checking opening hours with the university in advance, since it is a working scientific site, but the grounds and surrounding woods are pleasant on their own.
t.ancient city of sirwah@15.5,45.0:
Sirwah was a capital before Marib was. This ruined city on the edge of the Yemeni desert, east of Sanaa, was a major centre of the Sabaean kingdom in the first millennium BC, the culture that grew rich on the incense trade and later gave rise to the legend of the Queen of Sheba. The best known remains are the walls and the temple of Almaqah, the moon god of the Sabaeans, whose big oval wall of finely cut stone is inscribed with long lists of laws, treaties and victories. Together with the ancient dam at Marib, the group of sites is on the World Heritage list of Yemen.

The dam is the other great marvel. A huge earth and stone barrier built across a wadi, it stored seasonal floods and fed a network of irrigation canals that made the desert bloom, and its failure, around the sixth century AD, is remembered in the Quran and in Arab tradition as a great disaster. The sluices of the northern bank still stand, mighty blocks of stone worn smooth.

Yemen is in the middle of a long conflict, and the Marib region has been a front line, with fighting, mines and air strikes. Foreign governments advise against all travel, and there is no safe or sensible way to ride here, so this entry is for the memory and for the future. The roads are controlled by armed groups, fuel is scarce and checkpoints are many, and independent travel is not possible. Marib town, with seventeen thousand people in the recorded data, has grown enormously with displaced families, so the old numbers mean little.

If you want to understand the place while peace is out of reach, read about the Sabaeans, look at the photographs taken by archaeologists before the war and support the organisations working to protect Yemeni heritage. The landscape, with its dry red mountains, pale dunes and fortified tower houses, is among the most striking in Arabia, and there will be a day when travellers return. Until then, what remains is a map pin and the hope that the stones will survive.
t.dangyaband@38.8,48.7:
The Talysh lowlands of south-eastern Azerbaijan are the damp, green corner of the country, a narrow plain between the Caspian Sea and the Talysh mountains that run along the border with Iran. Dangyaband, near the village of Haftoni and about fifteen kilometres from Lankaran, sits in this world of rice, tea, citrus and hazel, where the climate is subtropical and the rain heavier than anywhere else in Azerbaijan. After the dry steppes of the centre and the oil-stained coast near Baku, it comes as a surprise.

Lankaran is a town of some two hundred and forty thousand people and the regional capital, with a long history as a Persian and Russian border port. Tea grew here in the Soviet period, and the region still produces it, along with lemons, tangerines and persimmons. The Talysh people have their own language, related to Persian, and their own traditions, including a taste for strong tea, smoked fish and dishes of rice and herbs, such as the dish called plov made with chestnuts or fish. Hirkan National Park, a relic forest of ancient trees such as Persian ironwood, covers the mountain slopes inland.

The riding is easy and quiet. The road from Baku runs south along the coast through flat farmland for about three hours, and the Lankaran plain has narrow, straight roads between fields, with mist in the morning and warm light in the evening. Rain is frequent, particularly in autumn, so carry waterproofs. Surfaces vary, with potholes and soft edges on smaller roads, and cattle and sheep wander on to the carriageway. The mountain roads that climb into Talysh are twistier and have more charm, with forest, small tea houses and views down to the sea.

Fuel is available in Lankaran and along the main road, but outside the town stations are few, so keep the tank topped. Food is simple and good, and a glass of tea in a roadside place is always welcome. Spring and early summer are the best seasons, when the plain is green and the air is mild.
t.saeen@38.0,47.9:
Sarein, spelled Sa'in or Saeen on various maps, is a hot-spring town in the Ardabil province of north-western Iran, set on the lower slopes of Mount Sabalan. Sabalan is a huge extinct volcano rising to about 4,800 metres, with a crater lake near the summit and snow that lingers into summer. The spring water here is naturally hot, rich in minerals, and has been used for bathing for centuries, with Iranian families coming from all over the country to bathe and picnic in the green meadows.

The region has a cooler, greener character than the deserts further south. Ardabil, about thirty kilometres east, is an old city on the plateau, famous as the home of the Safavid dynasty, which made Shia Islam the state religion of Iran in the sixteenth century. The shrine of Sheikh Safi al-Din, the founder of the Sufi order from which the dynasty grew, is a World Heritage site, a graceful ensemble of blue tilework, domes and gardens, with a collection of Chinese porcelain once kept there. The Ardabil carpets, among the greatest ever woven, take their name from the city.

The roads climb through rolling plateau and mountain scenery. The road from Ardabil to Sarein winds upward through meadows and low hills, with views of the great cone of Sabalan in good weather, and the air is noticeably cool. The surface is good on the main road, and curves become more frequent as the slope steepens. In winter snow and ice can close the higher roads, and fog is common in the valleys. Summer is the best season, when nomadic herders bring their flocks to the high pastures and the wildflowers bloom.

Fuel is available in Sarein and Ardabil, but the nearest listed village is some distance away, so fill up before heading into the mountains. The local specialities include honey, yogurt and a thick soup called ash, and you can often find a tea house with a view. Bring warm clothes even in July, because evenings are cold, and allow time for a long bath in the springs.
t.ruins and kilns@36.4,48.8:
Out on the high plain of Zanjan province, a long way from anywhere you might have heard of, there is a flat landscape of wheat fields and sheep pasture where the ground is strewn with brick fragments and bits of pottery. The label talks about ruins and kilns, and I should be honest that I cannot name the specific spot, but the setting is Soltaniyeh, the Ilkhanid capital that the Mongol ruler Oljeitu built in the early fourteenth century, and brick and ceramic making were central to its construction. A city that put up one of the largest brick domes in the world needed fired brick in huge quantities, and kilns on the plain would have worked day and night.

Soltaniyeh was founded by Oljeitu's father Arghun and finished by Oljeitu, a Mongol khan who had converted to Islam and wanted a capital to rival Tabriz, which was already a centre of the Ilkhanate. Its name means the imperial city. At its height it was an enormous settlement with gardens, bazaars and tents for the royal household, and for a few decades it was a stop on the Silk Road for merchants and ambassadors. After the Ilkhanate collapsed in the 1330s it declined, and most of the buildings fell into ruin or were quarried, leaving the great mausoleum standing like a lighthouse over the plain.

The plateau is high, around eighteen hundred metres, and the climate shows it: hot, dry summers, with cold winters and a lot of wind. Spring brings green wheat and wildflowers, and autumn a clear light that sharpens the dome from many kilometres away. The roads across the plain are straight and good, with the main highway from Zanjan to Abhar and Qazvin carrying heavy trucks, and quieter side roads linking the villages.

The nearest sizeable towns are Abhar, a little over thirty kilometres to the south-east, and Zanjan, some forty kilometres to the north-west, which has about three hundred and fifty thousand people. Fuel and basic food are available along the highway, and in Zanjan you can find hotels and restaurants. Zanjan is famous for its knives and for a type of handmade footwear, and its bazaar is a good place to wander. Carry water, and wear a scarf against wind and dust, because the plain gives no shelter.
t.soltaniyeh@36.4,48.8:
Soltaniyeh is the name of a small town on the plain between Zanjan and Abhar, and it is the name of one of the great buildings of Persia. The domed mausoleum of Oljeitu, finished in about 1313, rises from the plateau to around fifty metres, with a diameter of about twenty-five metres, making it the largest brick dome in the world at the time and a forerunner of the domes of Samarkand, Isfahan and even the Taj Mahal. It was listed by UNESCO in 2005, and when you see it from the highway, a pale turquoise-and-ochre bulk with eight slender minarets around its base, it looks too big for the landscape.

Oljeitu, or Öljeitü, was the Ilkhan, a Mongol ruler descended from Genghis Khan's grandson Hulagu, who governed Persia from the late thirteenth century. He is an intriguing figure, who tried several religions, including Buddhism and Christianity, before settling on Islam, first as a Sunni and later reportedly as a Shia, and he built the mausoleum possibly to house the remains of Imam Ali and Imam Husayn, a plan that was abandoned. After his death the building was used as his own tomb. The design uses a double-shell dome, a technical advance that influenced later Persian and Ottoman architecture.

Inside, the walls were covered with painted and tiled decoration, and parts of it survive, with geometric patterns, floral designs and calligraphy in bright colours. Galleries run around the upper levels, and visitors can climb to the top for a view of the plain. The restoration of recent decades has been extensive, and the exterior brick is cleaned and consolidated.

The road to it is simple, a short turn off the highway between Zanjan and Qazvin, through wheat fields and flat horizons. The land is high and open, and wind is a constant, so take care on exposed sections. Heavy trucks use the main road. The town of Soltaniyeh has a few shops and tea houses, but for fuel you should head to Abhar or Zanjan, each thirty to forty kilometres off. Foreign motorcyclists in Iran typically need paperwork such as a carnet and often a guide, so check current rules in advance. The best time is late spring or early autumn, when the light is clear and the ground is not baked or frozen.
t.fenjanabad@36.4,48.8:
Fenjanabad is a name I could not pin to a famous monument, and I would rather say so than invent one. It is in the Soltaniyeh area of Zanjan province, a piece of the high plain north-west of Abhar, and the coordinates fall within sight of the great Ilkhanid dome. So the useful thing to describe is the countryside that surrounds it: a basin about eighteen hundred metres above sea level, edged by low ridges that turn pink in the evening, and filled with villages of mud-brick houses, poplars along irrigation channels and fields of wheat, barley and sunflowers.

Villages like this have their own rhythm. In late spring the sheep and goats go out to the pasture on the hills, shepherded by men in felt hats, and in summer the farmers cut and thresh the grain, with the dust rising above the fields. Autumn brings the harvest of apples and walnuts from small orchards, and in winter a hard cold settles, with snow that can lie for weeks. The old irrigation system, with underground channels called qanats, still waters some fields, and you may see the line of mounds that mark them across the ground.

The history behind it all is that of Soltaniyeh, which was a royal capital for a short time in the fourteenth century. The Ilkhans, who were Mongols, kept herds on these plains and used them as summer pastures, since the grass here is excellent. In the evenings, when the plain is empty, you can imagine the tents of the court and the horses on the grass, and the dome in the distance catching the last sun. The place feels both remote and well known, because tour buses stop at the mausoleum and then leave.

The roads between villages are narrow, mostly asphalt but patched, with farm vehicles, motorbikes and flocks of sheep sharing the surface. Go slowly, and expect dogs to chase. The main highway has fuel and basic services at intervals, but the practical choices are Abhar to the south-east and Zanjan to the north-west, both thirty to forty kilometres off. Take water and food, and respect local customs, particularly modest dress and polite greetings. Tea is offered readily, and a few words of Persian will be appreciated.
t.karvangah@36.4,48.8:
Karvangah looks like a name from the old caravan roads, since the word seems to mean a place for caravans, and that is exactly the character of this part of Zanjan province. I cannot tell you what particular structure the label refers to, but the coordinates are on the plain at Soltaniyeh, on the historic corridor that linked Tabriz with Qazvin and Tehran, and merchants and pilgrims followed it for a thousand years. Tracks like this were studded with caravanserais, walled inns spaced a day's travel apart, with a gate, a courtyard, stables and rooms around it, and the Safavid shah Abbas I built dozens of them.

If you are riding here, that history shapes the road. The modern route from Qazvin to Zanjan and on to Tabriz follows the old line, climbing gently onto the plateau, passing through towns like Abhar and Soltaniyeh, and offering long straights and low passes. It is a big, fast road with a lot of lorry traffic, in which the main hazards are overtaking trucks and loose gravel at the edges. Away from the highway you meet narrow lanes between villages, with old brick walls and the occasional ruin of a caravanserai standing in a field.

The landscape is high steppe. In spring the plain is green with young wheat, and the hills behind are dotted with red tulips and poppies for a short time. By July it is brown and dry, with dust devils in the afternoon, and by November there may be snow. The light is the great reward here, especially at the edges of the day, when the dome of Soltaniyeh turns the colour of honey and the shadows stretch for miles.

Zanjan, about thirty-nine kilometres to the north-west, is the provincial capital, with some three hundred and fifty thousand people. It is known for its knife-makers, for its fine filigree silverwork, and for thick, flat bread baked in stone-lined ovens. Abhar is the nearer town on the other side and has fuel stations as well. The sensible rule for Iran applies: fill up whenever you see a station you trust, carry water and expect people to offer you tea with a smile.
t.chelebi oghlu@36.4,48.8:
Next to the great dome of Soltaniyeh stands a smaller building that tells another story, the tomb of Chelebi Oghlu. The name is Turkish and echoes the title Chelebi, which was used for the leaders of the Mevlevi order, the whirling dervishes who follow the poet Rumi, and Oghlu means son of. I cannot give you the full biography of the man buried here, and the sources I know are thin, but the building is a reminder that the Ilkhanid capital drew mystics as well as princes, and that Sufi lodges grew up near royal sites in the fourteenth century. A tomb in the shadow of the mausoleum was a mark of status for a holy man.

The building is a modest one, a square chamber topped by a dome, with a pointed entrance arch and some remains of glazed tilework in turquoise and dark blue. Brick is the main material, as everywhere on this plain, and the way it has been laid in patterns, in bands and diamonds, is a pleasure in itself. The surroundings are quiet, and you may find the doors locked and need to ask a local caretaker. Remember that this is a shrine, so dress modestly and take your shoes off if you go inside.

The plain here is high, flat and windy, and the horizon is huge. Roads between the tombs and the main highway are narrow, sometimes sandy at the edges, with the odd farm tractor or flock of sheep. You can ride a loop of the area in an hour, stopping for photographs, but the better way is to walk between the sites, since many are within sight of each other. Late afternoon gives the best light, with long shadows and the dome turning gold. In midsummer the sun is fierce, and by October the nights are already cold.

Fuel and meals are in Abhar or Zanjan, each about thirty-five kilometres away, and you should have a full tank before you come out. The village near the dome sells tea and simple snacks, and the owners may invite you to sit for a while. Carry water and a hat. If you have a spare hour, climb the stairs of the great mausoleum, and from the gallery look down on the little tomb and the patchwork of fields beyond.
t.mollah hassan kashi tomb@36.4,48.8:
The tomb of Mollah Hassan Kashi lies a short walk from the Soltaniyeh dome, a small square building with a conical or domed roof and a courtyard that has been a place of local pilgrimage for centuries. Kashi means from Kashan, the city famous for tilework, and the name suggests a scholar or religious teacher who came from there, a figure of the later Islamic centuries after the Ilkhanids had gone. I cannot say more about him with confidence, and I would rather you asked at the site than rely on a half-remembered date from me. What I do know is that the tombs of holy men and scholars gathered around Soltaniyeh long after the court had left, because the great mausoleum gave the place an air of sanctity.

Like many shrines in Iran, it works as a small community centre. People come to tie strips of cloth to the railing, to light a candle, or to sit and read the Quran in the shade. The tilework on the facade may include blue and green glaze in the Kashan tradition, and the decorative bands of calligraphy are worth a look. If the door is open, a visit takes only a few minutes, but the atmosphere of unhurried devotion is what stays with you.

Zanjan province has a cold continental climate, and the village near the shrine sits high on a plateau where winter can bring deep snow and spring thaws turn the tracks to mud. Mud-brick houses with flat roofs and chimneys cluster along the road, and storks nest on the old walls in spring. Rain is rare in summer, and the dust that blows across the plain coats the roadside bushes and the wing mirrors of passing trucks.

On a motorbike, the best approach is a slow ride around the farm tracks, with frequent stops. The main road is smooth but busy with trucks, so use the side lanes whenever possible, taking care at junctions where drivers rarely signal. Water points are scarce, so carry plenty. The nearest towns for fuel and meals are Abhar, about thirty-five kilometres off, and Zanjan, which is a bit further. In either, a plate of rice with grilled chicken and a glass of doogh, a salted yoghurt drink, will set you up for the afternoon.
t.tappeh nur kuchak@36.4,48.8:
A tappeh is a mound, and Iran is dotted with them. The word describes a low hill formed by thousands of years of settlement, as mud-brick houses collapsed and were rebuilt on top of their own remains, so that the mound grows slowly upward like a layered cake. Tappeh Nur Kuchak, which seems to mean little Nur mound, is one of a cluster of such hills on the plain of Soltaniyeh, in Zanjan province, and it is set among wheat fields a short distance from the great dome. I do not know what archaeologists have found here, and I will not guess, but the shape of the ground tells its own story: this plain was lived in long before the Mongols arrived.

The Zanjan plateau has a record of human settlement that goes back to the Neolithic, because the plain was fertile and the streams from the surrounding hills provided water. Over the millennia farmers, herders and traders left pottery, tools and burials, and the mounds around Soltaniyeh are the surface trace of that. When the Ilkhans chose the plain for their capital in the fourteenth century, they were choosing a place with a very long history of use. In that sense the mounds and the dome belong to the same landscape.

A mound like this is not much to look at, and a visitor may see only a grassy rise with a few sherds on the surface. The reward is the view from the top, a wide sweep of plain with the dome in the distance and the hills on either side. Please do not pick up artefacts, since removal damages the archaeology, and be aware that digging and metal detecting are illegal. Farmers use the land, and tracks cross it, so ask before entering fields.

The rough tracks are fine for a light bike in dry weather but turn to sticky mud after rain, so take care. The main roads are paved and fast, and fuel is in Abhar or Zanjan, each about thirty-five to forty kilometres away. A flask of tea and some bread are worth bringing, as there are few places to stop. Spring is the best time, when the grass is green and larks sing over the wheat, and the evenings are mild enough to sit on the mound and watch the sunset.
t.emamzadeh dur@36.4,48.8:
An emamzadeh is a shrine to a descendant of one of the Shia Imams, and Iran has thousands of them, from grand domed complexes to tiny whitewashed rooms beside a spring. Emamzadeh Dur stands in the countryside of Zanjan province, on the plain of Soltaniyeh, and I cannot tell you whose tomb it is or when it was built, only that such shrines tend to be much older than their present buildings and to have a cluster of legends attached to them. Locals often come to them with vows, to pray for a sick child or a good harvest, and you may see a sheep tethered outside, waiting to be sacrificed and shared with the poor.

Shrines like this are the real social centre of rural Iran. A typical one has a small dome of brick or tile, a courtyard with a tree and a well, and a sill where visitors leave coins or sweets. Women and men may enter by separate doors, and the green banners and the tinkling of a metal grille are signs that the place is cared for. As a visitor, you should be respectful: dress modestly, take your shoes off, and ask permission before taking pictures. A cheerful greeting in Persian goes a long way.

The surrounding plain is typical of the high plateau, with wheat and barley fields, rows of poplars along irrigation canals, and the dome of Soltaniyeh in the middle distance. Roads here are narrow, with potholes where the asphalt edges crumble, and the occasional donkey cart or flock of sheep can appear around a bend. The weather is cold in winter, sometimes below minus fifteen, and very pleasant in late spring, when the whole plain smells of cut grass and warm earth.

Practical points are simple. The nearest large town is Zanjan, thirty-seven kilometres away, which has fuel, hotels, restaurants and a fine bazaar, and Abhar is roughly the same distance in the other direction. There is nothing in the way of services at the shrine itself. If you reach it at midday you may find the courtyard empty and the door open, and you can sit in the shade with a flask of tea and listen to the wind in the leaves.
t.tappeh qal eh@36.5,48.8:
Qal'eh means fort or castle in Persian, and a tappeh qal'eh is a mound with a fort on it, or in this case a fort that has turned into a mound. The one on the Soltaniyeh plain in Zanjan province is a low rise in the fields, with no standing walls, only a faint rampart and a scatter of brick and pottery. I do not know the details of its excavation, and I will not make any up, but a fortified mound in this position would have watched over the plain and the road that ran across it, long before the Mongol khans built their capital here. In landscapes like this, forts are a constant, because the plateau was crossed by armies, caravans and nomads in every age.

The best way to read the place is to stand on top and look around. You see a flat, open plain, a little over eighteen hundred metres above the sea, with the Soltaniyeh dome to the south-east, ridges in the distance, and the line of the road. From such a mound, a guard could see a column of dust for kilometres, and a signal fire could pass a message across the whole plateau in a few hours. The geography explains why this region was disputed between Iran's neighbours for centuries, from Parthians and Romans to Seljuks and Mongols.

The ground around is farmland, and a visitor should keep to the tracks and respect crops. In spring the plain is patched with green and gold, and larks and hoopoes are easy to see. Summer is dry and dusty, and the shimmer of heat makes the dome seem to float. Winter brings snow, which can close minor roads, so be careful when choosing your season. Early autumn, with clear skies and a touch of gold on the poplars, is a lovely time.

Zanjan, about thirty-six kilometres to the north-west, is the place for fuel, meals and a bed, and it is a large, lively city with students and a bazaar full of knives and copperware. On the way you will pass roadside stalls selling honey, walnuts and dried fruit. A packet of local biscuits and a flask of tea make a good picnic. Carry plenty of water, since the plain has very little shade, and cover your head against the sun.
t.soltaniyeh pasture including mostafa kha:
The word pasture is the key to understanding why the Mongols came here. The Ilkhans, who ruled Persia from the thirteenth to the fourteenth century, were steppe people who kept great herds of horses and sheep, and they chose to build their capital on the plain of Soltaniyeh because it was good grass country, cool in summer and wide enough for a court on the move. The Soltaniyeh pasture is the open grassland around the dome, still grazed by flocks today, and it is part of the UNESCO listing because it is part of the historic landscape. The Mostafa Khan in the label may refer to a local structure or property, but I do not know its history, so I will leave it there.

Standing on the pasture, you see the logic of the place. The ground is flat and carries long grass in spring, a sea of green with poppies and wild tulips here and there, and the dome stands alone on the horizon. The court would have moved between winter quarters on the warm plains and summer quarters on the high ground, in a pattern the Mongols kept for generations.

Today shepherds in felt hats and rubber boots move their flocks across the area, with dogs, and sometimes a pickup carrying water barrels. The dogs can be fierce, so keep a distance and do not walk through a flock. Motorbikes are unusual here, and you may attract curiosity, and perhaps an invitation to tea at a black tent or a farmhouse. It is a pleasure to accept, though be ready for a long conversation in half-understood Persian and a lot of hand gestures.

The roads through the pasture are earth tracks, fine when dry and sticky when wet. Fuel and food are in Abhar, thirty-four kilometres off, and in Zanjan, a little further. Best to arrive early or late in the day, when the light is low and the shadows long. Bring water, a hat and sun cream, because the plain offers no shade at all, and keep an eye on the weather, since thunderstorms in late spring can build quickly over the hills and drop hail on the plateau.
t.qush khaneh@36.4,48.8:
Qush Khaneh is a name I can read but not fully explain. In the Turkic language of this region, which is widely spoken in Zanjan province, qush means bird, and khaneh is the Persian word for house, so it sounds like a bird house, which might point to a falconry building, a pigeon tower or a pavilion for keeping hunting birds. Mongol rulers loved falconry, and hunting parks and hawks were an important part of court life, so a structure of that kind near the Ilkhanid capital would not be surprising. But I do not have a reliable account of what is actually here, so I will describe the setting instead.

The plain around Soltaniyeh is a natural stage for birds. Larks and wheatears nest in the fields, and in spring, rollers and bee-eaters flash blue and green along the wires. Raptors hunt over the stubble, with kestrels hovering and the occasional eagle on a distant mound. In autumn flocks of migrating cranes and storks pass through, tracing a route between the Caspian and the interior. If you bring binoculars, you can spend an hour watching without leaving the track.

Pigeon towers, which are large, round, domed buildings full of nesting holes, were common in central Iran, built to collect droppings for fertiliser, especially for melon fields. The one at Meybod near Yazd is famous. In the Zanjan area, such towers are less common, but the principle of using birds in daily life is the same. A falcon on a gloved hand was a status symbol, and the feathers and skills of the royal falconers were an item of diplomacy between courts.

The ride around here is quiet. The roads off the highway are narrow, with farm vehicles and herds, and the surface can crumble at the edges, so slow down at bends. The wind often blows hard across the plain, and gusts can be strong on open stretches. The main highway has fuel stations, and the larger towns of Abhar and Zanjan, each about thirty-five to forty kilometres away, have everything else. Take a flask of tea, a hat and good sunglasses, because the light on the plateau is hard and white, and the dome shimmers in the heat.
t.soltaniyeh dome@36.4,48.8:
Stand beneath the dome of Soltaniyeh and look up. The inner surface rises in a great curve of brick and plaster, the proportions as calm as an egg, and the light falls from windows in the drum so that the whole interior seems to float. This is the mausoleum of Oljeitu, built between 1305 and 1313, and it is the oldest surviving double-shell dome in Persia. The outer shell is a tall, ribbed bulb covered in turquoise glaze, which once glittered across the plain like a jewel, and the inner shell is separated from it by a gap that kept the mass of the roof manageable. Around the base stand eight minarets, slender and decorated with tile, which have long since lost their tops.

The inside is much better than you expect from the plain exterior. In the main chamber, which is about twenty-five metres across, the walls carry stucco decoration of the Ilkhanid period, with Quranic inscriptions in Kufic script, and the traces of painted designs in red, blue and gold. An upper gallery wraps around the room, and the stairs lead up into the space between the shells, from which you can look down into the chamber and out over the plain. Parts of the structure have been strengthened after earthquakes, and visitors must obey the rules for what may be climbed and when.

Inside, sound behaves oddly. A voice in the middle of the floor echoes for several seconds, and a clap rings up into the dome, so people tend to speak in whispers. The interior is cool on a summer day and bitterly cold in winter, with a stone smell. A small museum in the lower crypt holds artefacts and photographs of the restoration, and the guards are often keen to show visitors the best views. Entry costs a modest fee, and foreigners pay more than locals.

The approach is simple, a short road from the highway, with a car park and a row of stalls selling tea, souvenirs and local sweets. Fuel is in Abhar or Zanjan, about thirty-six kilometres each way. Come in the morning if you can, because the light is better for photographs and the coaches have not arrived yet. If you can, return at sunset, when the dome turns copper and the plain turns violet, and the minarets stand out against a darkening sky.
t.lisar@37.9,48.8:
Lisar is a village in the Talesh mountains of Gilan province, in the north-west of Iran, where the high ridges fall steeply to the Caspian Sea and the sea clouds pile against the slopes. This is the wettest part of the country, and the hillsides are covered with Hyrcanian forest, an ancient broadleaf woodland of beech, hornbeam, oak and alder that survived the ice ages and is now recognised by UNESCO. In the mist the trees are draped with moss and the air smells of wet leaves, and after the dry brown plateau of central Iran it feels like another continent. A waterfall and a stream run through the area, and it is popular with walkers from the coastal towns.

The Talesh people have their own language and customs, closely related to other north-west Iranian languages, and the villages are scattered along the slopes with wooden houses, tin roofs and rice paddies in the valleys. Tea is grown on terraces in the lowlands, and the traditional dishes include smoked fish, walnut-and-pomegranate sauce and a dish of rice with local herbs. In summer, families from the hot plains come up to escape the heat, and the roads fill with cars at weekends.

The riding here is some of the best in the country, and quite different from the desert. The road from Hashtpar climbs into the hills with hairpin bends, forest on both sides, and cloud that can drop in a few minutes. The surface can be wet, with leaves and mud, and landslides after heavy rain are not rare. Cows and goats are common on the road, and fog turns bends into guesswork. The highway over the mountains from the coast towards Ardabil is a famous route, which in winter can be icy.

Hashtpar, seventeen kilometres away, is the town with fuel, shops and a market, and from there the coast road runs north to Astara on the Azerbaijan border, a busy trading town. In the hills, services are limited, so top up the tank below, and carry rain gear because sunshine can vanish suddenly. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with clearer skies and fewer people. In summer humidity is high, and mosquitoes near the paddies are tiresome.
t.seh tappeh@36.5,48.8:
Seh Tappeh means three mounds, and the name is a good description of what you see: a trio of low hills rising from the flat fields of the Soltaniyeh plain in Zanjan province. I do not have a reliable record of what excavation has revealed here, so I can only describe the setting. But the mounds are a good way to think about how this plateau was lived in. A tappeh does not appear overnight. A village of mud-brick houses stands for a century or two, the roofs fall in, the walls melt in the rain, and the next generation levels the rubble and builds again, over and over, until the hill is several metres high.

Because mud brick is made from local earth, a mound is in a sense just a small hill of the plain itself, remoulded by people. Scattered across its surface you may see bits of coarse pottery, charcoal and the odd animal bone, the debris of cooking and craft, and archaeologists read these like pages. The dating comes from the style of pots and from radiocarbon tests, and in this part of Iran the story runs from early farming villages in the sixth millennium BC through the Bronze and Iron Ages, with later habitation overlaying the earlier. The trio near Soltaniyeh is probably a small cluster of such settlements.

The mounds are on private farmland, so ask before crossing fields. In a dry year, the crops are thin and the track is dusty, while in a wet spring the plain turns green and the surface can be slippery. The wind is a constant companion, and sometimes a cold one, because the plateau is high. A walk to the top takes a few minutes and gives you a view across the fields to the dome, which seems to rise from the grain.

The nearest big town is Zanjan, thirty-five kilometres to the north-west, where you can find fuel, a hotel and a good meal, and the road there passes through villages with roadside stands selling walnuts and honey. Abhar is also within reach. Carry water, wear a hat and keep to the tracks, and if a farmer waves you over, you may be offered a glass of tea and an apple, which is the proper end to the visit.
t.tappeh dur@36.4,48.8:
Dur is a Persian word for far, and Tappeh Dur, the far mound, is one of those cheerful names that tell you a village once stood on the edge of someone's territory. It lies on the plain of Soltaniyeh in Zanjan province, among fields of wheat and barley, one more low rise in a country of low rises. I cannot give you its excavation history, so instead let me explain what such a place can tell a visitor with sharp eyes, because that makes the stop worth the walk.

Start with the ground itself. Mud-brick walls, when they collapse, leave a characteristic yellow-grey earth, and among it you can find bits of fired pottery, often with painted bands or burnished surfaces. Old ploughing breaks the surface and turns up fragments, and after a rain the colours stand out. Look for the flat pieces of grinding stone, black flint blades used in sickles and the gleam of a glazed fragment from later periods. All of these are small pieces of life: a pot for water, a blade for harvest, a grinder for bread.

The location tells another story. The plain is watered by seasonal streams from the surrounding hills and by wells, and it offered grazing and soil for early farmers. When the Ilkhans arrived in the fourteenth century, they found a land already scored by centuries of human use. The mounds, the dome and the dry watercourses form a single record, though most visitors see only the dome. Taking time with the mounds, even for twenty minutes, deepens the visit.

Access is by farm track, and the surface can be rough. In dry weather a small motorcycle manages easily, but after rain the clay becomes sticky and slippery. The nearest towns for fuel and food are Zanjan to the north-west, about thirty-seven kilometres, and Abhar in the opposite direction, just a little further. Spring is the best season, with green wheat and singing larks, but late autumn has a beautiful light. Bring water and food, and leave every sherd where you find it, so that the next visitor can read the same page.
t.tappeh nur@36.4,48.8:
The plain of Soltaniyeh is a working landscape, and Tappeh Nur, the mound of light, sits right in the middle of it, with wheat or barley growing around its base. The name Nur is a common one in Persian, and I would not pin it to any particular story. The mound is one of several close to the dome, and like its neighbours it marks a settlement of the distant past, whose details I cannot supply. What I can tell you is what the farmers do, because the people who work these fields are the real guardians of the site.

In the Zanjan plain, grain is the main crop. Wheat is sown in autumn or early spring, and it ripens in June, when the whole plain turns gold and combine harvesters crawl across the fields in clouds of dust. After the harvest, flocks are brought in to graze on the stubble, and the straw is baled for winter feed. Alfalfa is grown for fodder, and potatoes, sunflowers and sugar beet appear in rotation. Irrigation is by pumps from deep wells, which has lowered the water table in recent decades, a problem across much of Iran.

For a rider this is quiet, open country, with long straight roads and almost no traffic on the side lanes. The wind is nearly always present, and in spring it can be bitterly cold on the high plain even when the sun is out. Tracks to the mounds are unpaved, and you should stay on them rather than ride across crops. Dogs guard the flocks, and they can be aggressive, so keep your distance and do not stop beside a flock.

Abhar, about thirty-five kilometres to the south-east, has fuel stations and a market, and Zanjan, a bit further north-west, has a full range of services and a lively bazaar. On the way, look for roadside stalls selling local honey and walnuts. A picnic on the top of the mound, with bread, cheese and cucumbers, is a pleasant way to take in the view, and the dome of Soltaniyeh appears in the distance, pale against the hills. Take your litter with you, and watch for scorpions under flat stones.
t.coyhaique@-45.6,-72.1:
Coyhaique is the biggest town in Chile's Aysén region, and where the Carretera Austral really starts to feel like a frontier. It sits in a green valley at the meeting of two rivers, the Coyhaique and the Simpson, with steep forested ridges all around and a distinctive pentagonal main square. People here are used to long distances and bad weather, and the town has the practical feel of a place that serves the farms, fishing villages and mountain lodges strung out along the highway.

Built mostly by army engineers from the 1970s through the 1990s, it was designed to connect isolated settlements in Chilean Patagonia that otherwise could be reached only by boat, plane or horse. It runs for about twelve hundred kilometres from Puerto Montt to Villa O'Higgins, a mix of tarmac, gravel and ferry crossings, through temperate rainforest, past glaciers, fjords and blue-green lakes.

South of Coyhaique, the road is a delight and a challenge. There is paved road for some distance, then gravel for long stretches, with loose stone, corrugations, and dust in dry weather, mud in wet. Weather changes quickly, so carry waterproofs and warm layers even in summer. The best months are December to March, when days are long, though rain is still common. Wind can be fierce along open stretches, and traffic is light, so rest stops and mechanics are far apart.

Coyhaique has fuel, supermarkets, banks, workshops and a good range of lodging, and it is the last big place for resupply before the long southern stretches. Fill the tank and carry a spare can before heading south, because the next reliable pumps may be a long way off. Try Patagonian lamb roasted over an open fire, and buy bread and snacks for the road. Check ferry timetables and gravel conditions locally.
t.puerto rio tranquilo@-46.6,-72.7:
Puerto Río Tranquilo is a small settlement on the western shore of Lago General Carrera, the vast lake that Chile shares with Argentina, where it is known as Lago Buenos Aires. The water here has a startling colour, a milky turquoise caused by glacial flour, and the lake is so big that the far shore is lost in haze. The village itself is a handful of streets with wooden houses, guesthouses and boat operators, and a population of only a few hundred.

What draws people are the Marble Chapels, the Capillas de Mármol, a set of caves and pillars carved by the lake's waves out of a marble outcrop on the shore. Seen from a small boat, the swirling blue and white walls glow in the reflected turquoise of the water, and in calm weather you can glide right inside the caverns. Mornings are best, when the lake is flat and the light is good, while wind in the afternoon can cancel trips. The surrounding mountains hold the Northern Patagonian Ice Field, and valleys nearby lead to glaciers such as Exploradores.

The road here is the Carretera Austral, and this section from Coyhaique is among its most beautiful. It runs past Cerro Castillo, whose jagged spires stand above the road, then follows the lake shore with great views. Most of it is gravel, with corrugations, loose stones and dust, and long exposed stretches where the wind can be fierce. In rain, the surface turns slick and muddy. Distances between settlements are large, and weather changes fast, so carry waterproofs and warm clothing. The best months are December to March, though even then rain and cold are possible.

Fuel is the thing to plan. There may be a pump in the village, but supplies can run out, so fill the tank in Coyhaique and carry a spare can. There are simple restaurants and guesthouses, though rooms fill quickly in summer, so book ahead. Try lamb cooked over an open fire, fresh trout, and warm bread from a local bakery.
t.caleta tortel@-47.8,-73.5:
Caleta Tortel has no streets. The village hangs off the rocky shore of a fjord in southern Chilean Patagonia, and everything, from the church to the post office to the family houses, is joined by boardwalks and stairways of cypress timber that rise and fall with the slope. Wheels are left at the top, and so are motorbikes, because the whole place is a footpath. The wood is the local ciprés de las Guaitecas, which resists rot in the constant rain, and the walkways give off a damp, resinous smell that you notice as soon as you step off the road.

The setting is wild. The Baker river, the largest in Chile by volume, pours out of the Patagonian ice fields to the east and meets the sea here in a wide delta, in a milky blue-green colour from glacial silt. Islands and channels lie to the west, and cloud sits on the forested hills for days at a time. The ice fields themselves, huge remnants of the last ice age, are a short boat trip away. Rain falls on most days of the year, so a good set of waterproofs is more important than the choice of tyres.

Getting here is part of the story. The Carretera Austral, the gravel highway built through the region in the late twentieth century, leaves its main line near Cochrane, and a branch road of some twenty kilometres drops down to the village, ending at a car park above the settlement. The surface is gravel, sometimes loose, and the way is narrow and winding, with sharp bends and drops. After rain, take it slowly and watch for trucks. The summer months from December to March are the most comfortable and the roads are best.

Small guesthouses and a few places to eat serve fish, bread and strong tea, and you should book ahead in the high season. Leave time to walk to the end of the boardwalks, then sit, listen to the water, and consider the way a community has been built without a single street.
t.cerro castillo@-46.1,-72.1:
The mountain that gives this village its name looks like exactly what it is called, a castle. The jagged ridge of Cerro Castillo rises above the Carretera Austral in a crown of dark towers and spires, streaked with snow and hanging glaciers, and from the road it fills the sky. It lies in the Aysén region of Chilean Patagonia, about a hundred kilometres south of Coyhaique, and the surrounding national reserve protects the peaks, lakes and valleys beneath. The village at its foot is small, with a few guesthouses and a place or two to eat, and it exists mostly because the road stops here.

The country around is open and wind-swept. The Carretera Austral, built through the mountains over several decades and still gravel in many sections, runs through steppe and southern beech forest, with the sky wide and the weather moving fast. Guanacos, slender relatives of the llama, graze on the hillsides, and condors circle overhead. To the east the road toward Lago General Carrera, one of the largest lakes in South America, drops down in bends with views of impossibly turquoise water. Dust, loose gravel and strong crosswinds are typical, so ride with a loose grip and keep speed under control.

Practical care is essential. Distances between services are long, and fuel supplies can be thin or irregular, so fill up at Coyhaique, the regional capital, before heading south, and carry a reserve if you can. Tyres take a beating on this surface, and the nearest repair shop might be a long way off. Rain and cold can arrive in any season, and even in summer, from December to February, nights are cool. A windproof layer is the single most useful piece of kit.

The local culture is rooted in cattle and sheep, and gauchos on horseback are a regular sight on the roads. Many travellers also walk the trail around the base of the peaks, a multi-day route that passes a turquoise lagoon beneath the ridge. If time is short, an hour's walk up the valley behind the village gives a good view of the towers. Eat a hot meal in the village, because food gets simple further south.
t.armenian monastic ensembles of iran@39.0:
The Aras river is a hard border here, a green-brown ribbon in a gorge with fences and watchtowers on one bank and the mountains of north-western Iran on the other. At this point you look from the Azerbaijani exclave of Nakhchivan across to the Iranian side, where a group of Armenian monasteries sits in country that Armenians have called home for nearly two thousand years. UNESCO lists them together as the Armenian Monastic Ensembles of Iran: the Monastery of Saint Thaddeus, the Monastery of Saint Stepanos, and the chapel of Dzordzor.

Saint Stepanos is the one you can see best from here. It stands in the Aras gorge itself, a small fortress-like complex of warm stone in a dry canyon with cliffs rising on both sides, and it is still the setting for a pilgrimage and for Armenian services. The architecture combines the steep conical domes and carved stone of the Armenian tradition with a Persian taste for decoration in the details, a mix that makes the whole group unusual. Keep in mind that you are looking at a sensitive frontier. Photography near the river is tolerated in some places and frowned upon in others, and soldiers are never far, so be polite and do not point a long lens at anything with a flag.

The ride around here is a dry upland one. The road along the Aras runs through bare hills of ochre and grey rock, with narrow irrigated strips where poplars and orchards cling to the river. Wind is common, the sun is hard, and winters bring snow on the higher passes and a bitter cold on the plateau. Late spring and early autumn are the sensible seasons. The Aras valley is known for its birdlife, and in spring the gorge fills with swifts and bee-eaters.

Culfa, called Julfa in the old spelling, lies about fourteen kilometres away and has roughly ten thousand people, fuel and basic food. The town once had a famous medieval cemetery of carved stone crosses, the khachkars, which was destroyed in the early 2000s, a loss that still weighs on the region's memory. Border permits and visa matters are strict in this corner, so check your papers well before you plan to reach the river, and do not expect smooth improvisation.
t.darresham chapel@39.0,45.5:
The chapel of Dzordzor sits in a narrow valley of north-western Iran, a small Armenian church in country where the hills fold into one another and the villages are few. The name in Persian is Darresham, and the site belongs to the same UNESCO group as the great monasteries of Saint Thaddeus and Saint Stepanos. It is the smallest of the three, but it carries the same quality of stubborn survival: a stone building, rebuilt and repaired by the community that depended on it, still standing in a landscape where most of the evidence of earlier lives has been scraped away.

The pin on this map falls near the Aras river on the Azerbaijani side of the frontier, so for a rider the practical picture is the borderland: red-brown hills, dry stream beds, a river that flows brown in spring and thin in autumn, and farmland in the valley bottoms. The air smells of dust and wild thyme, and in early summer the slopes carry a thin cover of grass that bleaches fast. If you are heading into Iran proper, the road toward Khoy runs through this sort of country, with long gentle gradients and tight bends where it crosses a ridge, and you meet more shepherds than traffic.

The local culture is a layered one. Armenians, Azeris and Kurds have lived side by side in this part of Iran for centuries, and each group left its mark: churches with conical domes, mosques with blue tilework, caravanserais along the old trade road from Tabriz to the Black Sea. The Armenian community here once ran schools and workshops and now numbers far fewer people than it did, which is part of why the chapels matter so much to those who remain. Pilgrims still come at set times of year, bringing food and candles, and the valley comes briefly alive.

Plan fuel carefully. The nearest town with services on this side of the river is Culfa, about sixteen kilometres away, and Khoy, a large Iranian city, is a long way to the south. Water bottles and some food are sensible, because villages here do not have shops open all day. Spring is the best time, when the hills turn green and the roads are dry. Autumn is calm. Winter is cold, windy and sometimes impassable, so leave it to people with local help and studded tyres.
t.the main church@39.0,45.5:
The Monastery of Saint Thaddeus is known locally as Qara Kelisa, the Black Church, and the name comes from the dark stone used in its lower walls, set against lighter stone above. It stands in the hills of north-western Iran, in West Azerbaijan province, in a green valley where the road runs between orchards and low ridges. Tradition says that the apostle Thaddeus founded a church here in the first century and was buried on the spot, and while no one can prove that, the site has been a place of Armenian pilgrimage for many centuries.

The buildings you see now are far younger and belong mostly to the medieval period, rebuilt after earthquakes and repaired in later ages. The main church is a compact, strong structure, with steep roofs and a central dome, and its walls carry delicate carved reliefs of saints and animals. Inside it is cool, dim and quiet. Once a year, in July, Armenians from across Iran and beyond gather here for a major feast with pilgrims sleeping in tents around the walls, and the surrounding fields are full of music, smoke from cooking fires and the sound of children. At other times of year, the place can be completely empty, with only a caretaker and the wind.

The roads here are the long climbing roads of the Iranian north-west: wide valleys with irrigated fields, then tighter sections as they pass over ridges. The surface is usually fine on main roads and rough on village tracks. The weather is the main variable. Summers are dry and hot, snow arrives in November and stays until March at height, and spring rain can turn a dirt lane to mud. The pin on this map sits near the Aras river, some way off, so treat the monastery itself as lying further inland among the hills of Chaldoran.

Fuel and shops are found in the larger towns, and the border town of Culfa, about fourteen kilometres from the pin, is the nearest point of any size on this side. For the Iranian side, Khoy and Maku have all the supplies you could need. Visitors should dress modestly, women covering their hair when they enter, and ask before taking photographs inside. A small donation is a courtesy, and a patient walk around the outside walls is worth more time than a quick look at the doorway.
t.cochrane@-47.3,-72.6:
Cochrane is the town you remember because it is the last proper one. South of here the Carretera Austral thins out into a road with more rivers than villages, and the whole way down to Villa O'Higgins it will be mostly gravel, with only a few small settlements. Cochrane has around three thousand people, a tidy square, a handful of hospedajes and shops, and one of the last reliable fuel pumps in the region, so this is where you fill up and eat something properly before continuing.

The town sits on the shore of Lago Cochrane, called Lago Pueyrredón on the Argentine side, a big blue lake that straddles the border. Nearby is the Río Baker, which carries more water than any other river in Chile, a startlingly pale turquoise as it leaves the lake, and the confluence with the Neff river is a good stop on the way south. t.villa o higgins@-48.5,-72.6:

t.jamal abad@37.3,47.8:
Jamal Abad lies in the highlands of north-western Iran, in the Azerbaijan region, a country of rolling steppe, bare hills and high plateaus between the cities of Zanjan and Tabriz. The villages are built of mud brick and stone, with flat roofs, and flocks of sheep and goats move across the slopes in the care of shepherds. I cannot tell you about a particular landmark at this spot, so I will describe what lies around it.

The ride that includes it heads north toward Ardabil, where the Sheikh Safi al-Din Khanegah, a Sufi shrine of the fourteenth century, stands in a walled garden. t.el chalten@-49.3,-72.9:
El Chaltén is a young town in a very old landscape. It was founded in 1985, partly to establish an Argentine presence in a region disputed with Chile, and today it is the trekking capital of Argentina, a small cluster of lodges, cafes and gear shops beneath the granite spires of the Fitz Roy massif. The surface is paved, but the wind is the real obstacle. Patagonian gusts can blow riders across the lane, and a loaded bike is a sail. Lean into it, stay relaxed on the bars and pick the calmer early hours when you can.

Even in January, the weather can swing from sun to sleet in an afternoon, so carry waterproofs and warm layers, and keep gloves handy. Summer daylight lasts until late in the evening, which gives the long ride a generous window.

Fuel is the practical question. The town has a small station, but supplies have been known to run short in busy seasons, so the sensible approach is to fill the tank in El Calafate before the run and again at the first opportunity after. Food in El Chaltén is excellent for a town of its size, with hearty Patagonian lamb, trout, empanadas and craft beer, and the evening crowd of hikers swaps stories over dinner.

The surrounding land is part of Los Glaciares National Park, a World Heritage Site, with the great Southern Patagonian Ice Field to the west. A short walk from town leads to viewpoints of Fitz Roy and Cerro Torre, and early mornings, when the peaks glow orange, are worth getting up for.
t.fianarantsoa@-21.5,47.1:
Fianarantsoa sits in the middle of Madagascar's southern highlands, and the name is usually translated as the place where one learns what is good. It is the capital of the Betsileo people, a population of rice farmers whose terraced hillsides you will have been riding through for the last hundred kilometres, and the old upper town, perched on a ridge above the modern one, still has the stone houses and church spires that the nineteenth century left behind. The riding is the reason most people come. The RN7 from Antsirabe has been climbing and dropping through villages built of red brick and clay, with rice paddies stepping down every slope, and from Fianarantsoa it continues through hills toward Ambalavao and then the open plateau. The tarmac is narrow, patched and shared with pousse-pousse, bush taxis, zebu carts and lorries that do not hurry. Ride slowly. Potholes appear around blind bends, and children and chickens treat the verge as a living room. Daylight is short in the tropics, so aim to be parked before dusk, because nobody enjoys this road in the dark.

The town is also the starting point for the little train that runs east to Manakara, the old French line that goes down through the forest to the coast, a trip that people often tell you is more journey than railway. Tea and coffee grow on the hills nearby, and the area has a long history of wine production, thin and sweet, from vineyards that missionaries started. Whether you want to drink it is a personal matter.

t.isalo@-22.5,45.4:
Isalo is the end of the long southbound haul down the RN7, and the landscape changes abruptly to mark it. After the green terraces of the highlands the road enters a country of dry grass, scattered palms and then, suddenly, a sandstone massif that rises like a ruined wall out of the plain. The Isalo range is a mass of Jurassic sandstone that wind and rain have carved into canyons, buttresses and bare orange ridges, with narrow green oases hidden between them where water still runs all year.

Along the way you pass Ranohira, a town of around six thousand people that has the last real services before the park, including fuel, which is worth knowing because the miles beyond it toward Ilakaka and Toliara are long and thin on supplies. Ilakaka itself, further on, is a sapphire boomtown that appeared in the late nineties, and has the frontier look of a place that grew in a hurry.

You may see ring-tailed lemurs in the trees near the trails, along with sifakas, and in the evening the ridge lines turn a deep red. The Bara people who live in this region have a tradition of burying their dead in rock crevices in the sandstone, so ask before photographing anything that looks like a tomb.

The weather is dry for much of the year, hot in the afternoon and cold at night, and the rains from about December to March make parts of the area muddy and the light dramatic. Dust is a nuisance on the road shoulders. When you arrive, find a place with cold water and a bed, take the helmet off and let the quiet of the rocks settle in. After a ride like the RN7, that is the right way to finish it.
t.chupan chapel@39.0,45.6:
I have to be straight about this one: the Chupan Chapel is not a place I can describe in any detail, and I would rather say so than invent it. What I can tell you is the country around it. The pin falls in the Julfa district of Nakhchivan, the Azerbaijani exclave that is cut off from the rest of the country by Armenia, in a dry, rocky corner of the South Caucasus where the Aras river forms the border with Iran. The word chupan, as far as I know, means shepherd in the Turkic and Persian languages of the region, which fits the high, grazed slopes around.

Alinja Castle, near Julfa, is a medieval hilltop fortress on a steep rock, with views over the valley. Local tradition places Noah's landing here after the flood, and the name of the main city is sometimes linked to that story. The climate is continental, with hot dry summers and cold winters, and the sky is usually clear.

The roads along the Aras and into the mountains are generally paved but narrow, and the roads climb in bends through arid hills with long views, but surfaces can be patchy and livestock wander freely. Frontier zones near the Iranian border have checkpoints and restrictions, so carry passports and documents and do not wander near the border without permission. Travel into Nakhchivan itself involves flying or crossing through Iran or Turkey, so check visa and vehicle rules in advance.

Practically, Culfa has fuel and basic shops, and Yaycı and Sumbatan-diza are smaller villages with little. In the towns, restaurants serve kebabs, lamb stews, bread baked in clay ovens and strong tea in small glasses. Bring water and sun protection, and get an early start, since midday heat on the bare hills is severe. If you find the chapel, enjoy the silence, and treat it with respect as a place of worship.
t.noravank@39.7,45.2:
The red cliffs of the Amaghu gorge close in around you for the last few kilometres, and then Noravank appears, a small honey-coloured church perched against a wall of rust-coloured rock. The name means new monastery, though it was founded in the thirteenth century, and it stands in the Vayots Dzor province in southern Armenia, in a dry, rocky country of canyons, vineyards and apricot orchards. The setting is a large part of the effect. Crimson cliffs rise on both sides, the stream runs far below, and the church looks as though it grew from the stone.

The star building is the church of the Holy Mother of God, built in the early fourteenth century by the architect and sculptor Momik, who is buried nearby. It has two storeys, with a narrow exterior staircase leading to the upper level, a feature that was unusual in Armenian architecture, and the carvings on the facade, with their delicate reliefs of saints and angels, are among the finest of the period. Momik also carved some of the most beautiful khachkars in the country, and a famous one stands in the grounds. The Orbelian princes, who ruled the region, had Noravank as their family burial place, and the monastery became a centre of learning.

The road in is the final part of the ride, a narrow, twisting road that follows the gorge. It is a mixture of good tarmac and rough patches, with sharp bends, falling rock and the occasional herd of goats. It is worth taking slowly, partly for safety and partly for the view of the cliffs changing colour in the light. Early morning is best, before the tour buses arrive and when the cliffs glow, and in late afternoon the light turns the rock deep red.

In a cave near Areni, a few kilometres away, archaeologists found the remains of a wine press and fermentation vessels about six thousand years old, as well as a leather shoe thought to be older than Stonehenge. Local winemakers use native grapes such as Areni, and a glass of the red, with its dark cherry taste, is a pleasant reward at the end of the day. Apricots, the national fruit, are in season in July.

Areni, six kilometres away, has a few small shops and wine houses, and Yeghegnadzor, twelve kilometres away, has fuel and larger markets. There is nothing on the road to the monastery itself except a small kiosk, so bring water, and a hat in summer, since it gets hot.
t.selim pass@39.9,45.2:
At 2,410 metres, the Selim Pass is the high point of the old road between Lake Sevan and the Vayots Dzor valley, and it is a stern, beautiful place. The pass crosses the Vardenis range, a line of bare volcanic mountains, and the road climbs in long bends through rolling alpine meadows, where the grass is cropped short by sheep and the wind blows steadily. At the top, the scenery is open and empty, with no trees, only grass, rocks and sky, and the visibility on a clear day is enormous.

The road follows an ancient line. For centuries, caravans carrying silk, spices and other goods crossed here on their way between Persia and the Black Sea, and the pass was one of the key links on that branch of the Silk Road. Remains of the route can still be seen in places, and the pass is dotted with cairns and crosses. Travellers on this high road needed shelter, and the caravanserai at the summit, built in the fourteenth century, provided it.

Conditions can change in minutes. The pass is open in summer, usually from May or June until October, but heavy snow can close it from late autumn to spring, and storms can sweep in even in July, with cold rain, hail and low cloud. Dress for cold and wet, and check the weather before starting. Fog is common, and in bad visibility the road is hard to follow, with few barriers and steep drops on the outside of some bends. The surface is a mixture of tarmac and broken patches, so watch for potholes. A good, well-paced approach rewards you.

Wildlife is part of the show. Griffon vultures and eagles ride the winds, and marmots whistle from the rocks. In spring and early summer the meadows burst with flowers, including poppies and gentians. Shepherds bring their flocks up from the valleys for the summer pastures, and you may find sheepdogs, which are large and serious, watching you from the roadside. Treat them politely.

The nearest villages, Yeghegis and Shatin, have little more than a shop, and the nearest town with proper services is Karanlukh, or Yeghegnadzor, in the valley. Fill up before you climb, carry water and a layer, and take your time. A stop at the summit, with the wind at your back and the whole of the range spread out beneath you, is a good reward.
t.orbelian caravanserai@39.9,45.2:
Beside the road at the top of the pass, a squat building of dark basalt sits low in the grass, and it is one of the best-preserved caravanserais in Armenia. The Orbelian Caravanserai was built in 1332 by Prince Chesar Orbelian, who ruled the region, to give shelter to merchants crossing the mountains on the Silk Road. An inscription over the door records the date and the builder, in the Armenian of a prince who knew the value of being remembered. Travellers paid nothing, and the prince's purpose was as much pious as commercial.

Inside, the building is more impressive than the outside suggests. A low entrance leads into a long hall with three aisles, divided by rows of pillars supporting a vaulted ceiling, and a small opening in the roof lets in daylight and lets out smoke. Stone mangers line the walls for animals, and raised platforms were used as sleeping places for the people. The atmosphere is cool, dim and a little eerie, and it is easy to imagine camels, mules and merchants huddled here against the snow. Water drips from the roof after rain, and the smell is of old stone and damp earth.

It was a place of safety on a dangerous crossing. The pass is high, cold and storm-prone, and before roads were built, travellers could be trapped here for days. In bad weather, a caravanserai could mean the difference between life and death. Most such buildings along the Silk Road have been ruined or lost, but this one survived, and it has been carefully looked after ever since.

Outside, the ground is open and rolling, and on a clear day you can see far across the mountains. Some visitors picnic by the walls, and sheep graze the slopes nearby. The air is thin, and a brisk wind blows nearly always, so a windproof layer is wise. Do not count on any stall being open.

Yeghegis and Shatin, about thirteen kilometres away in the valley, offer simple shops, and Karanlukh, eighteen kilometres on, has fuel and more choice. Bring your own water and food, and make sure the tank is full before the climb. A torch is useful in the dark interior.
t.perito moreno@-46.6,-70.9:
Perito Moreno is a small town in the north-west of Santa Cruz province, on the edge of the Patagonian steppe, and it has nothing to do with the famous glacier except the name.
