t.kazan observatory@55.8,49.1:
Kazan is the capital of Tatarstan, and the point at these coordinates sits in the old university quarter, close to the Kremlin walls, where the city's scientific history is concentrated. The university, founded in 1804, grew into one of the leading centres of learning in the Russian Empire, and its astronomical observatory, established in the 1830s, was one of the first in the country. Founded about a thousand years ago and capital of a Tatar khanate until Ivan the Terrible stormed it in 1552, Kazan has a white-walled Kremlin containing both an Orthodox cathedral and the Qol Sharif Mosque, rebuilt in the 2000s with bright blue domes. Streets are lined with merchant houses, and Tatar food, including chak-chak, a sweet of fried dough and honey, and echpochmak, a triangular meat pie, is easy to find. The best season is May to September, and the city is a pleasure in the long evening light, though winters are bitterly cold.

Fuel, food and lodging are plentiful, and the city has no shortage of petrol stations, cafés and hotels. For a break, the pedestrian street of Bauman is lively, and local cafés serve good coffee and pastries.

Spend an evening here. The old town glows, and the river is just a few minutes away.
t.bolgar@55.0,49.1:
Bolgar is the place where Islam came to Russia, or at least to the middle Volga, in the year 922. The ruler of the Volga Bulgars, Almish, asked the Caliph of Baghdad for help in building a fortress and teaching the faith, and the caliph sent an embassy, which included the traveller Ibn Fadlan, whose account of the journey is a key source on early medieval life along the river. The Mongols sacked it in the thirteenth century, and later it became a quiet backwater.

What remains is a remarkable complex of stone buildings on a low terrace above the Volga. A tall, squat minaret from the thirteenth or fourteenth century stands among the ruins, along with a mausoleum, the Black Chamber, and the remains of baths and a mosque. Nearby, a modern white mosque, completed in 2012, rises above the site, and a museum explains the history. The Bolgar Historical and Archaeological Complex has been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 2014, and for many Tatars it is a symbol of their roots, and a pilgrimage destination. On a summer evening, the golden light on the old brick is lovely.

You see the Volga as a wide silver band, and the sky is large. Traffic is moderate, with trucks and sometimes slow farm vehicles, and the weather is variable, with hot summers and fierce winters. The best months are May to September.

Fuel and food are simple. The town of Bolgar has a few stations and shops, and Tetyushi, about fifteen kilometres away, is bigger. Tatar cafés serve soup, noodles, meat pies and tea, and you should try the local pastries. Many visitors arrive by river boat from Kazan, which is a pleasant way to see the landscape.

Walk among the ruins in the late afternoon. The wide river below, and the pale stone, have a gentle beauty.
t.taltal@-25.4,-70.5:

Morning fog can reduce visibility, but by midday the sun is high and the colours sharpen: pale tan hills, deep blue sea and bright green patches where cactuses cling to the slopes. Walk to the end of the pier at sunset, when the fishermen are mending nets and the light turns the water pink, and you will understand why people stay.
t.perito moreno town@-46.6,-70.9:
Perito Moreno is a town of about three and a half thousand people in the north of Santa Cruz province, and it is not to be confused with the famous glacier of the same name far to the south. Even without leaving the town, you feel the age and scale of this country, where the horizon is as far away as it gets. It is a place to stop, refuel and take stock before the next long stretch.
t.los antiguos@-46.5,-71.6:
Los Antiguos is the improbable orchard of Patagonia. The name means the ancient ones, a reference to the Tehuelche people who once lived and hunted here.

Wind is the main factor, and it can be ferocious across the open plain, so keep your grip firm. The bends are few and gentle, the surface good, and the traffic light. As you approach the town, the colour changes dramatically, with lines of poplars, green fields and the first shade you have seen for a long way.

Check the opening hours before you go.

The lake itself is one of the largest in South America, shared between Argentina and Chile, and its colour shifts from deep blue to milky green depending on the light. In the evening, when the wind drops, the mountains on the far side glow pink and the surface turns to glass. Walk down to the shore, take off your gloves and dip a hand in the cold water. t.bajo caracoles@-47.5,-70.9:
Bajo Caracoles is hardly a town at all, and that is exactly why it is famous. Out on the Patagonian steppe in northern Santa Cruz, on one of the most remote stretches of Ruta 40, a handful of buildings stand beside the road: an old general store and hotel, a fuel pump, a few houses and a lot of sky. Its name, meaning low place of the snails, refers to the fossil shells found in the surrounding ground, and the whole area is a dry seabed that was lifted up when the Andes formed.

Wind is constant, and can blow so hard that the dust hangs sideways across the road. The distances between settlements are enormous, so the pump and the tiny shop here are among the few places for hundreds of kilometres where you can count on anything, though supplies can run out and the pump is not always open, so carry spare fuel and food and ask in advance if you can.

The old hotel and store have been a stop for travellers for almost a century, and the bar, with its walls covered in stickers and messages from passing riders, is a place to sit and swap stories. Spring and autumn can bring snow and ice, so the best months are December to February. A night here, with the wind outside, is one of the true Patagonian experiences.
t.gobernador gregores@-48.8,-70.2:

It sits on a broad, wind-swept plateau of steppe, where sheep farming has been the main business since the early twentieth century, and the nearby estancias, some of them enormous, sprawl across tens of thousands of hectares. Fill the tank and bring food and water, because the next settlements are far apart. Meals tend to be simple and filling, with meat, pasta and a bottle of local wine. t.titi@37.0,49.9:
Gilan, on the Caspian shore of Iran, is the wet side of the country, a strip of rice paddies, tea terraces and thick forest squeezed between the sea and the Alborz mountains, and the Titi label sits in it, about twenty-five kilometres from the town of Astaneh-ye Ashrafiyeh and not much further from Langarud and Rudsar. Oak, hornbeam, beech and the ironwood tree grow here, along with leopards, brown bears and a rich bird life, though a visitor will mostly see mushrooms, mosses and mud. The castles named on your ride are mountain strongholds of Gilan's past, reached by long climbs. Rudkhan Castle, near Fuman, is a brick and stone fortress with dozens of towers laid across a wooded ridge, and the walk up takes a good while on steps.

The riding is the main attraction. The old coastal road along the Caspian is flat, humid and busy, with many villages, markets and small towns, while the roads climbing into the hills offer tight bends and great scenery, though also slick surfaces, fallen leaves and, often, fog. Rain can be heavy at any time of year, but especially in autumn, so a good waterproof is as important as sunglasses. Landslides are possible after storms. Spring brings blossom and rich green, while late summer is hot and sticky.

Gilan has its own cooking, with smoked fish, walnut and pomegranate sauces, garlic and herbs, and the aubergine dish mirza ghasemi, served with bread. Tea is grown at Lahijan and taken in small glasses, often with sugar lumps. Astaneh-ye Ashrafiyeh, with about forty thousand people, has fuel and shops, and Langarud and Rudsar are also larger towns with services. Roads through the villages are narrow, and local drivers can be fast and impatient, so ride carefully, and check the rules for foreign travellers before you plan a trip.
t.assumption cathedral and monastery of th:
Sviyazhsk is an island town, or nearly so: a green hill rising from the Volga where the Sviyaga river joins it, with a low causeway tying it to the mainland. Ivan the Terrible had it built in 1551, in a matter of weeks according to the chronicles, using timber floated down the river from Uglich, as a forward base for his campaign against the Khanate of Kazan. The assault on Kazan succeeded the next year, and the little fortress town stayed on as a monastery and administrative centre for centuries.

At its heart stands the Assumption Cathedral and monastery, a sixteenth-century church with later additions and some remarkable frescoes, including a famous one of Saint Christopher shown with a dog's head, which is an Eastern Orthodox oddity. UNESCO inscribed the site in 2017. The island became truly an island only in the 1950s, when the Kuybyshev reservoir rose and flooded the lowlands around the hill, which is why the view over open water is so wide today.

The approach is easy and flat. From Kazan, about thirty kilometres to the east, you drive through farmland and low wooded hills, and Vasilyevo, a town of around sixteen thousand, is the nearest place for fuel and a proper meal. The last stretch crosses a causeway, with water on both sides and a wind that can be strong, so keep a firm grip when trucks pass. You leave the bike outside and walk the little streets, where cafés, craft stalls and wooden houses sit among the monastery walls.

Go early on a weekday to avoid tour groups, because Sviyazhsk is popular with visitors from Kazan and beyond. Summer evenings are lovely, with a long, soft light over the reservoir, while winter is stark and quiet. The Tatar and Russian histories meet here in a way that is rare, and the town carries it with ease: a place for slow walking, a long look at the water, and a bowl of something hot before you ride on.
t.historic and architectural complex of th:
Kazan's kremlin stands on a white-stone hill above the Kazanka river, near its meeting with the Volga, and its walls and towers enclose some of the oldest and most dramatic stories of the Tatar people. The fortress was the heart of the Khanate of Kazan, one of the successor states of the Golden Horde, until Ivan the Terrible besieged and stormed it in 1552, an event that opened the Volga to Russian expansion. In the centuries after, the Russians rebuilt the place in their own style, so that today it is a meeting of two worlds: the Annunciation Cathedral with its green domes and the great mosque, side by side.

The mosque is the Qolşärif, rebuilt and opened in 2005 for the millennium of the city, with a high white-and-blue structure and minarets that rise above the walls. It stands on the site of a mosque that was destroyed in the conquest, and it is a statement of Tatar identity as well as a place of prayer. A nearby leaning tower, named after Söyembikä, a queen of Kazan, is the kremlin's most famous symbol, though the stories about it are more legend than record. The complex was listed by UNESCO in 2000.

Kazan today is a city of over a million, lively, young and proud of its mixed Tatar and Russian character. The streets below the kremlin are full of cafes, and the pedestrian street of Bauman is where people stroll in the evening. The local food is rich and good: chak-chak, a sticky honey sweet; echpochmak, a triangular pie of meat and potato; and strong tea. Traditional tea houses serve all these in a warm, relaxed manner.

Riding in the centre of Kazan is not a pleasure, since traffic is heavy, parking near the kremlin is limited and the streets are busy with trams, buses and cars. The best approach is to leave the bike in a car park and enter on foot. Outside the city, the Volga plains are flat, wide and agricultural, with long straight roads and fields of sunflower and wheat. Fuel is available everywhere in the city and its suburbs. Summers are warm, with long evenings, and winters are bitterly cold, with snow and ice, so the riding season runs from May to September.
t.kazan@55.8,49.1:
Kazan sits where the Kazanka river meets the Volga, and the Tatars who live there like to say that their city is Russia's third capital, a claim made with a straight face and a little provocation. It is the capital of Tatarstan, a republic of about four million people with its own language, a Muslim and Orthodox Christian population that lives side by side, and a food culture that sets it apart from the rest of the country. The Kremlin, on a hill above the river, was added to the World Heritage list in 2000, and holds both the Annunciation Cathedral, built after Ivan the Terrible's conquest in 1552 by masters from Pskov, and the Qolsarif mosque, with its blue minarets, rebuilt in the 2000s on the site of the one destroyed in the conquest.

The leaning Soyembika Tower, a slim brick tower, is the city's emblem, and it carries a legend about a queen who threw herself from its top rather than marry the conqueror. Beyond the Kremlin, the pedestrian Bauman Street, lined with shops, cafes and a statue or two, leads to the old Tatar quarter across the Kaban lake, where wooden houses with carved eaves and mosques give a feel of another time. In the evening, the long promenade along the river and the great Millennium Bridge glow with light.

A day ride out of Kazan takes in the broad river country of the Volga. The roads run across rolling farmland, with wheat fields and birch woods in every direction, and the main highways are wide and in decent condition, though trucks are thick. Out on the minor roads, the surface may break up, with potholes after winter, and villages have speed bumps. In summer the days are warm and long, and thunderstorms can roll in late in the afternoon. Autumn gives clear air and golden leaves, while winter brings deep cold, with snow and ice that make riding impractical.

Kazan has many fuel stations, shops and hotels, and traffic in the centre is heavy at rush hour, so aim to leave early. Try echpochmak, a triangular pastry filled with meat and potato, and chak-chak, a dessert of fried dough strands bound in honey, and tea is always served strong and sweet. The people are famously hospitable, and a cafe stop turns into a conversation easily. Check the current travel advice for the region before you go, as conditions and rules for visitors can change.
t.goujebel@38.3,46.9:
Ahar is a town in the north-west of Iran, in East Azerbaijan province, and the hills around it are the southern edge of the Arasbaran, a mountainous forested region that drops toward the Aras river and the border with Azerbaijan and Armenia. At the coordinates for Goujebel, you are in a landscape of rolling grassy hills, scattered villages, fruit orchards and patches of oak woodland, with stone-walled fields and, in the distance, ridges that turn blue with haze in the afternoon. I do not know a specific monument at this spot and I would rather be honest than fill the space with guesses, so this is a description of the region and what a rider will find there.

The Arasbaran has been recognised as a biosphere reserve, valued for its mix of forest and steppe, where brown bears, wild boar, deer and many birds live in relative peace, and where the villagers still keep sheep and bees. Honey from this region is highly regarded, and so are the walnuts and the walnut-and-cheese pastries you can find in small shops. The people here are Azeri Turks, and you will hear Azerbaijani Turkish spoken far more than Persian, a point of pride and a language you might try greeting people in.

The riding is a delight if you like quiet roads. Beyond Ahar, narrow asphalt lanes wind through the hills, climbing gently from valley to valley with unbroken views over green slopes in spring and golden stubble in late summer. The surface can be patchy and edges crumble, and animals wander across, so keep your speed modest. Winters are cold and snowy, with drifts that close the higher lanes, while summer is warm but comfortable at altitude. The best season is late spring, when the hills are green and wildflowers appear.

Ahar, with over ninety thousand people, is the place to stock up: it has fuel, bakeries, tea houses and simple restaurants serving grilled meat, dizi stew and plenty of flatbread. Beyond it the villages are small, with limited facilities, so carry some water and cash. Not far away rises Babak Castle near Kaleybar, a mountaintop fortress linked to the medieval rebel leader Babak Khorramdin, a place that draws trekkers and history lovers alike.

If you are travelling in this region, remember that border areas can have checkpoints, so keep your passport handy and ask locally about any restricted zones before leaving the main roads.
t.ranomafana@-21.3,47.5:
Ranomafana means hot water in Malagasy, and the name is a clue to the place. The village sits in a steep, forested valley on the escarpment that drops from Madagascar's central highlands toward the east coast, where the Namorona river drops over rapids and hot springs seep from the rock. The surrounding national park, created in 1991, protects some of the island's most important rainforest, and in 2007 it was added to a UNESCO listing of the rainforests of the Atsinanana. Mist hangs in the trees, orchids cling to the branches, and the air is warm and damp.

The park is famous for lemurs. In 1986, the American scientist Patricia Wright found a species of golden bamboo lemur here, a small, russet animal that feeds on giant bamboo and had been unknown to science, and the find led directly to the creation of the park. A walk of an hour or two with a guide will probably reveal several species, from red-fronted brown lemurs to the tiny mouse lemurs at night, along with chameleons, frogs and a huge range of insects. The local Tanala people, whose name means forest people, have lived here for centuries.

The road to Ranomafana is a challenge and a reward. From the main highway, the RN7, which runs from Antananarivo south to Fianarantsoa and on toward Toliara, a branch road winds east through tea country and into the forest, with sharp bends, potholes and trucks heavily laden with produce. Rain is frequent, particularly between November and March, and the surface can be slick. In the dry season, from April to October, the roads are better, but the nights in the mountains are cold. Take your time and watch for children and zebu on the road.

Fuel is not available in the village, so fill at Fianarantsoa, the nearest large town, and carry a small reserve. Simple hotels and small restaurants serve rice, zebu and vegetables, and in the evening you can sit in the thermal pool if the water is running. Carry cash in Malagasy ariary, since cards are of little use, and bring waterproofs and leech socks if you plan to walk in the forest. The reward for the effort is a rainforest that few riders ever see.
t.astronomical observatories of kazan fede:
Kazan University has a claim to a surprising scientific lineage. The Russian mathematician Nikolai Lobachevsky, who worked out a geometry in which parallel lines behave differently from the ones taught in school, was a professor here and later its rector, and the university built an astronomical observatory in the nineteenth century. The observatories of Kazan Federal University grew from that early effort, and one of them, the Engelhardt Observatory, was founded outside the city by a Russian nobleman and amateur astronomer who gave his instruments to the university. It is a quiet place of domes and old telescopes.

Kazan itself is a bright, handsome, slightly surprising place, where two cultures share the same streets. The city sits on the Volga where the Kazanka River joins it, and it was the capital of a Tatar khanate before Ivan the Terrible took it in 1552. Today the white-walled Kremlin has a Russian Orthodox cathedral and the blue-and-white Kul Sharif Mosque side by side, a statement about coexistence that the city is proud of. Tatars are Muslims, speak a Turkic language and form about half the population of the republic.

The Tatar food is a pleasure. Echpochmak, a triangular pie filled with meat and potato, is the classic snack, and chak-chak, a heap of fried dough drenched in honey, is the sweet that goes with strong tea. Bauman Street, a long pedestrian lane in the centre, is the city's promenade, lined with cafes and statues, and the embankment on the Kazanka is a favoured evening walk. Kazan was named the third capital of Russia in a marketing campaign, which locals mention with a smile, and it hosted the Summer Universiade in 2013 and matches of the football World Cup in 2018.

Traffic in the city is heavy, and parking near the centre is difficult. Fuel is no problem in a city of over a million. The roads in the surrounding Tatarstan countryside are flat and straight, with farmland and birch forests stretching to the horizon, and the Volga is wide and slow. Summers are warm, and winters are hard, with snow and ice from November to March. Check current travel advice and entry rules before planning a trip to the region, since conditions can change.
t.kazan city astronomical observatory@55.8:
The Kazan city observatory belongs to the same story of science and empire as the university, but its charm is in the details. Astronomers in the city have studied the sky for two centuries, and their work gave Kazan a reputation as one of the intellectual centres of Russia east of Moscow. The observatories that survive are small and old-fashioned, domes on top of university buildings, and they mark Kazan's place as a university town and as a bridge between Europe and Asia.

The rest of the city is worth the time. The old Tatar quarter, Staro-Tatarskaya Sloboda, lies on the shores of Lake Kaban and has wooden houses with carved window frames, and a number of mosques, including the Marjani Mosque, a pale pink building of the eighteenth century. The Annunciation Cathedral in the Kremlin was built in the sixteenth century, and the leaning Soyembika Tower in the Kremlin is the city's emblem, with a legend about a queen who threw herself from it to avoid marrying Ivan the Terrible. The tale is more romance than record, but it is told with enthusiasm.

For riders, Kazan is the starting point of a ride westward along the Volga to the island town of Sviyazhsk, and to the Assumption Cathedral and Monastery, a group of buildings on a hill in the river, listed by UNESCO in 2017. The road runs through low hills, farmland and small villages, with a few bends and pleasant views of the Volga reservoir. Surfaces are generally decent, though they vary, and heavy trucks use the main routes. Wind off the water can be stiff.

Verkhniy Uslon, a town of a few thousand people on the opposite bank of the Volga, has shops and fuel. In Kazan itself, stations are plentiful on the ring roads. Take a lunch of Tatar noodle soup, called tokmach, or ask for a plate of baursak, little fried dough balls, with tea. Spring and early autumn are the nicest seasons. Always check current travel conditions and rules for visitors.
t.bolgar historical and archaeological com:
On a bank of the Volga, about a hundred and forty kilometres south of Kazan, stand the white remains of a medieval city that was once the capital of the Volga Bulgars. In 922 their ruler adopted Islam, and the northernmost Muslim state of its time grew up here, trading furs, honey and slaves with Persia and the Baltic. The Mongols sacked it in the thirteenth century, and it survived under the Golden Horde as a centre of Muslim culture, before fading as Kazan took its place. Today the site is a World Heritage property and a pilgrimage point for the Tatars, who regard it as the cradle of their faith and identity.

The ruins stretch across a meadow above the river. The most striking structure is the Small Minaret, a brick tower from the fourteenth century that leans slightly, with the Black Chamber, the Khan's mausoleum, the White Mosque and the stone remains of bathhouses nearby. A big new mosque in white stone, built after the fall of the Soviet Union, stands among them, and the Memorial Sign, a monument shaped like a Koran, honours the adoption of Islam. Behind the old walls, a museum holds finds from the excavations, including coins, jewellery and ornate pottery.

The riding up from Kazan is a long and easy day on flat roads that cross the wide Volga region, a landscape of wheat fields, birch belts and low hills. The road along the Kuybyshev reservoir has the huge expanse of the river on one side, with a very big sky, and the traffic is dominated by lorries and farm vehicles. The surface varies from smooth to rough, and the speed cameras are common near villages. Heat in July can be strong, and the wind off the water can make the ride cooler. Thunderstorms in summer can be violent.

Bolgar is a small town with about eight thousand people, and has basic fuel, shops and cafes, with Tetyushi to the south as a larger option. Tatar cooking is worth the stop, with chak-chak, a honey-soaked pastry, and echpochmak, a triangular pie of meat and potato, being the standard items. Early morning, when the white walls catch the sun and the tour buses have not yet arrived, is the best time to walk the site. Check current rules on travel and vehicle documents for foreign visitors in Russia before you plan.
t.area 1@55.0,49.1:
The label here is just a number, but the coordinates are exact enough to tell you where you are: on the left bank of the Volga near Bolgar, in Tatarstan, where the river has been dammed into the long, sprawling Kuybyshev reservoir. Before the dam was built in the 1950s the river ran narrower and faster, and the ruins of the medieval city stood further above the water. Today the shoreline is a gentle mix of sandbanks, reedbeds, birch and willow, and the water on a calm summer evening is the colour of pewter.

What interests a rider more than the ruins, perhaps, is the country around them. Tatarstan is a rich agricultural republic, and the road network is better than you might expect, with new surfaces and wide shoulders on the main routes and a web of side roads between villages. The rolling land, black earth and fields of sunflower, rape and wheat give a patchwork of yellow, green and gold, and in late summer the combine harvesters are out on every slope. Villages are marked by painted wooden houses with carved eaves, and by the green-domed mosques, which are as typical as the Orthodox churches of the neighbouring regions. This mixture of Islam and Orthodox Christianity is a source of local pride, and Tatars and Russians have lived together for centuries.

Kazan, with its Kremlin, mosque and lively streets, is the natural starting point, and the road down the Volga passes the island town of Sviyazhsk, founded by Ivan the Terrible in 1551 as a base for the conquest of Kazan, with a monastery on a green island. The road to Bolgar runs through the town of Zelenodolsk and then along the river, with wide views across the water. A day on the road can pass without much traffic, apart from slow farm vehicles, and the main hazards are potholes at the edge, livestock and the sudden showers that blow in from the west.

Bolgar, about three kilometres from the coordinates, has fuel and food, while Tetyushi is the next larger town. Fill the tank before leaving the main road. A glass of strong black tea with a sweet pastry, taken at a roadside cafe, is part of the local style. Be sure to check the current rules for foreign travellers and vehicles in Russia before planning a trip here.
t.center@38.1,46.3:
Tabriz is one of the oldest cities in Iran, and it feels like it. It sits at about 1,350 metres in the north-west, in a basin under the volcanic bulk of Mount Sahand, which rises to some 3,700 metres and holds snow well into summer. The city has been a capital many times: of the Mongol Ilkhanids in the thirteenth century, when it became one of the most important cities in the world, and of the first Safavid shah, Ismail, in 1501. The Ottoman armies took it and lost it repeatedly, and earthquakes, notably those of 1721 and 1780, flattened large parts, which is why so little of the old city survives above the ground.

Marco Polo passed through and praised its trade, and the bazaar tells you why. Tabriz carpets are among the most prized in Persia, with fine knots and floral patterns, and the city is known for its sweets, its meatballs called kofte Tabrizi, and its dairy, including the salty cheese of the nearby village of Lighvan. The people speak Azeri Turkish, and the culture is closer to Anatolia and the Caucasus than to Tehran. Tea is drunk from small glasses with sugar cubes held in the mouth, and strangers are likely to be invited for a cup.

Riding out of Tabriz is rewarding once you are away from the ring roads. The road south toward Kandovan, a village of rock-cut houses in strange conical formations, climbs through hills of yellow grass, and the roads north into Arasbaran, with its oak forests, offer cool air and winding bends. Winters are cold and snowy, summers hot and dry, and the best months are May, June, September and October. Traffic in the city is heavy and drivers are assertive, so patience helps.

Everything you need is here: fuel stations on every main road, workshops, restaurants and hotels. In a city of 1.4 million, you will have no trouble finding a place for a bike, and many hotels have secure yards. Start early to avoid the traffic, and before you leave, make time to walk through the bazaar and sit in a teahouse. It is one of the great experiences of Iran.
t.kabood mosque@38.1,46.3:
The Blue Mosque of Tabriz, known as the Kabood or Goy Masjid, was finished in 1465 under Jahan Shah, the ruler of the Qara Qoyunlu dynasty, who made Tabriz his capital. In its day it was said to be one of the most beautiful buildings in the Islamic world, covered in glazed tiles of deep turquoise and blue, with gold lettering, and the traveller who saw it called it the turquoise of Islam. An earthquake in 1779 brought it down, and what you see now is the result of a long restoration in the twentieth century.

The façade is the best part. The entrance portal is a tall, pointed arch with a rich mosaic of tiles in blues, greens and white, and inside, the main hall has a central dome and lots of fine tilework with a floral design. The dome chamber was built to be an extraordinary space, and parts of the original tiles can still be seen on the walls. A garden-like courtyard outside offers a place to sit, and the whole is easy to visit in about an hour.

The mosque stands about a kilometre from the centre of Tabriz, in an old quarter where streets are narrow and congested, with a good deal of one-way traffic. On a bike it is easy to get close, but you will probably have to leave it on the street or in a car park nearby. Plan to arrive in the morning, when the light on the tiles is best and the crowd is thinner. Dress modestly, and women will need to cover their hair.

Tabriz has fuel stations on every main road, and a wide range of food and lodging. Near the mosque, small tea houses sell strong tea, sweets and bread with cheese and walnuts, and in the evening the nearby streets fill with families. If you come in winter, bring warm clothes, as the climate here is cold and dry, and spring brings the freshest air. Photography is generally allowed inside the mosque, but ask first if you are unsure.
t.sorkhab@38.1,46.3:
Sorkhab is a district of Tabriz, in the east of the city, and its name means red water, said to come from the colour of a stream that once ran through the area. Today it is best known as a quiet burial ground, the Maqbaratoshoara or Mausoleum of the Poets, where many of the city's great writers lie. The most famous is perhaps Khaqani, the twelfth-century court poet of Shirvan, and the cemetery also has Qatran Tabrizi, who wrote in the eleventh century, and Shahriar, the twentieth-century poet who wrote in both Persian and Azeri Turkish and died in 1988.

The place is a garden as much as a graveyard, with shady paths, rose bushes, benches and carved stones. A modern memorial hall with a domed roof stands at its centre, and visitors come to read poems at the graves, which is a common thing in Iran, where verse is part of daily conversation. It is a calm, pleasant place, a sort of antidote to the bazaar's crowds, and the cypress trees give a bit of shade in the heat.

The district lies on the slopes of the city's eastern side, not far from the old centre, in a mixture of residential streets and small shops. Traffic can be heavy in the mornings and evenings, but at midday it is easier to move. Most streets are narrow and one-way, so park the bike outside and walk. The summer sun is strong, and winters can be bitterly cold, with snow on the roads, which is a reason to visit in spring or early autumn.

Tabriz, with nearly a million and a half people, has no shortage of fuel stations and food. Near the Mausoleum you will find small cafés where students gather over tea, and bakeries selling fresh bread. If you are interested in poetry, a short visit is rewarding, and even without Persian you can feel the respect with which people stand at the graves. Dress modestly, speak quietly and take your time. Keep a few small coins for the caretaker, who will often offer help.
t.tabriz historic bazaar complex@38.1,46.3:
The Tabriz Historic Bazaar Complex is one of the largest covered markets in the world, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2010. Tabriz has been a trading city since antiquity, sitting on the Silk Road between Asia and Europe, and its merchants were known to medieval travellers. The brick-vaulted halls that survive today mostly date from the eighteenth century, after the great earthquake of 1780, but the pattern goes back much further, with domed halls called timcheh, courtyards called sarai and long, covered passages, each devoted to a different trade.

Walk in and you are in a maze of brick arches, lit by shafts of light from small openings in the domes, and filled with the smell of spices, leather, rosewater and tea. The Timcheh-ye Mozaffarieh is a domed hall where carpets are sold, spread over the floor and hung from the walls, and it is a good place to learn about knots and dyes from sellers who will happily explain. Other halls sell gold, shoes, copper, hats, nuts and dried fruit, and a bazaar tea house is a good place to rest, with its samovar and sugar cubes. The call to prayer drifts through the halls.

Riding to the bazaar is a matter of arriving and parking. The area around it is a congested knot of narrow streets, one-way systems and pedestrians, so it is wise to park on the edge, in a car park or at a hotel, and walk the last part. Friday is the weekly holiday, when most of the bazaar is closed and the streets are quiet, so aim for another day. In summer, it is cool inside, and in winter it offers shelter from the cold.

Fuel and food are readily available across a city of 1.4 million, with filling stations on all main roads. After the bazaar, a bowl of abgoosht, a hearty meat and chickpea stew served in a small pot, is a perfect meal, and the sweets from the old shops make good gifts. Keep an eye on your belongings in the crowd, and be ready to haggle politely. Accept the offer of tea, which is part of the business of buying.
t.ancient dam of ma rib northern bank@15.4:
Eight kilometers from the modern town of Ma'rib, where the Wadi Dhana comes out of the hills into the desert plain, the northern end of the ancient dam still stands. It is a ruin of cut stone and carved channels, but it is a ruin of an engineering marvel. The Sabaeans, who ruled this part of southern Arabia from the first millennium BC, built a great earthen dam across the wadi to catch the seasonal floods, and at either end they placed sluice structures of finely worked stone to let the water out into canals.

On the northern bank you find the sluice gate and spillway, built of large blocks fitted with great care, and inscriptions in the Sabaean script that record repairs and the names of rulers who carried them out. The channels once fed a wide network of fields, and the oasis around Ma'rib was famous for its fertility and for the frankincense and myrrh that passed through it on the way north. The Qur'an alludes to the story of the dam's collapse, the flood of the Arim, which tradition places in the sixth century AD and which scattered the people of Saba across Arabia.

The surroundings are stark and beautiful. Dark hills rise on both sides of the wadi, the sky is hard blue and the ground between the stones is pale. In the early morning the light is warm on the masonry, and the valley is silent apart from the wind. It is easy to imagine the water roaring through the gate, and the farmland beyond.

An honest word is needed about travel. Yemen has been at war since 2014, and Ma'rib governorate has been a front line, with fighting, mines and air strikes. Foreign governments advise against all travel there, and this is not a place where anyone should plan to ride. These notes describe a place of history, and the situation on the ground should be checked with reliable current sources before any thought of visiting.

In peaceful times the road from Sana'a, about a hundred and thirty kilometers west, crossed desert and mountains, and Ma'rib offered fuel, simple food and a place to sleep. The dam itself is a short drive from town, and a morning is enough to see it.
t.awam temple@15.4,45.4:
Locals call it Mahram Bilqis, the sanctuary of the Queen of Sheba, though the real name of the builders' god was Almaqah, the moon deity of the Sabaeans. The Awwam Temple stands in the sands a few kilometers south-east of Ma'rib, a huge oval enclosure with walls of fine stone and a row of tall pillars that rise out of the sand like the teeth of a comb. It is among the largest and oldest religious sites in southern Arabia, built around the seventh century BC and used for well over a thousand years.

Most of the structure still lies under sand, and excavations have uncovered a wide oval wall, a portico with eight tall monolithic pillars and an inner courtyard that once held altars and offerings. Inscriptions record the rulers who restored and expanded it, and a necropolis nearby holds thousands of graves. For ancient pilgrims, it was the heart of a religious calendar tied to the harvest and the moon. Foreign archaeologists did substantial work here in the twentieth century, including a team from the American Foundation for the Study of Man in the 1950s.

The setting is stark, and that is its power. The temple sits in open desert, with flat ground in every direction and hills in the distance, and the pillars cast long shadows in the early and late hours. The stones glow warm yellow in the evening, and the wind carries a faint scent of dust and old stone.

The question of access has to be faced directly. Ma'rib has been a conflict zone for years, with fighting and risks that go far beyond ordinary travel concerns, and the area around the temple has seen damage and military use. Foreign governments advise against travel, and no rider should plan a visit without trusted, current local information, which at present suggests staying away. Think of the temple, for now, as something to read about rather than to ride to.

When conditions allowed, visitors came from Ma'rib town, which offered fuel, tea and small restaurants, and many hired a local driver with a four-wheel-drive for the short sandy approach. Bring water, a hat and a great deal of patience with the sun.
t.ancient city of ma rib@15.4,45.3:
Old Ma'rib rises from the plain as a pile of mud-brick towers on a low hill, a reminder that the city has been inhabited, abandoned and reborn many times. The ancient city was the capital of Saba, the kingdom that built its wealth on the incense trade and on the irrigation of the oasis. Here, the caravans bearing frankincense and myrrh from the coast of Hadramawt and Dhofar turned north toward Petra and Gaza, and the toll collected from them paid for temples, walls and an extensive water system.

Within the circuit of the old city, the remains of Sabaean walls, towers and houses can be seen, while the medieval mud-brick buildings stand on top of earlier ones. Tall houses with narrow windows and decorated parapets, like those of Sana'a and Shibam, grew here out of the same tradition of building with earth. The hill was abandoned in the twentieth century when the families moved to newer homes below, and the old town gradually decayed, leaving silent lanes and half-collapsed upper floors. Archaeologists have found Sabaean inscriptions in the stones of later buildings, a sign of how every age reused the one before.

The story most people carry in their heads is that of the Queen of Sheba, who in the Bible and the Qur'an visits Solomon with a caravan of gifts. Whether she lived in Ma'rib is a matter of tradition rather than proof, but the ruins give weight to the legend, and local people still speak of Bilqis with pride.

The reality of today must be stated plainly. The Ma'rib area has been affected by the war that began in 2014, with front lines nearby, and many displaced families now live in camps around the city. Travel advice from foreign governments is against any visit. The old city, with its fragile mud buildings, has suffered neglect and damage, and anyone considering the region should rely on up-to-date reports rather than old guidebooks.

In better years, a morning wandering the lanes, followed by tea in the new town, was a classic part of a trip from Sana'a. Fuel and food were available in the new town, and the roads from the capital crossed barren mountains with some grand views.
t.ancient dam of ma rib southern bank@15.4:
The southern end of the Ma'rib dam is the quieter twin of the northern one, and it is the place that makes clearest how the whole scheme worked. Across the Wadi Dhana, the Sabaeans raised a long earthen embankment, and on the south bank they built a stone sluice complex and a system of channels that sent the flood water into the fields on that side. The stones are huge and neatly dressed, and the walls curve around the spillway in a way that suggests careful hydraulic planning.

The dam is usually dated to around the eighth or seventh century BC, and it was repaired and raised over the following centuries. Inscriptions on the stones, in the elegant angular script of ancient South Arabia, record these works and name the rulers who ordered them. At its height the system irrigated a large oasis, and writers in antiquity described Arabia Felix, happy Arabia, as a land of gardens and rich harvests. Some of that reputation must have come from this valley. Around the sixth century AD the dam broke for the last time, and the community of the oasis, already weakened by political troubles, never fully recovered.

The ruins are impressive in the sheer scale of the effort. Standing on the southern sluice and looking across the dry bed of the wadi, the northern gate is visible in the distance, a reminder of how large the structure was. A modern dam was built upstream in the 1980s with help from the United Arab Emirates, named after Sheikh Zayed, and it now holds back water that the ancient builders would have recognized as a gift.

Visiting is a different matter. Ma'rib has been a battleground in Yemen's civil war, and the region has seen fighting, displacement and risk. Foreign governments advise against travel, and no one should plan to ride here without up-to-date information, which currently says stay away. It is better to remember the place through its history.

If the situation improves, the site is a short drive from Ma'rib town, where fuel and basic food were once available. Go early to avoid the heat, and bring plenty of water.
t.landmarks of the ancient kingdom of saba:
The kingdom of Saba, or Sheba, is among the oldest names in the history of Arabia, and its landmarks are scattered across the desert margin around Ma'rib. They form a group that includes the great dam, the temples of Awwam and Barran, the old city, and the sites of Sirwah and others in the highlands. Together they illustrate a civilization that rose around the first millennium BC by harnessing floodwater and controlling the incense route, one of the busiest trade arteries of the ancient world.

Incense was the engine of the economy. Frankincense and myrrh, gathered in the dry hills of Hadramawt and Dhofar, were in demand in temples and palaces from Egypt to Rome, and camel caravans carried them north through oases like this one. Saba taxed the trade and spent the proceeds on stone temples, canals and walls. The Sabaeans left thousands of inscriptions in their own script, many of them on bronze plaques and stone, and these give historians an unusually detailed view of kings, gods and irrigation rights.

The landscape between the sites is austere and wide. The Ramlat as-Sab'atayn desert lies to the east, the highlands rise to the west, and between them the wadi systems carve out the corridors where people lived. In the heat of day, the horizon shimmers, and in the evening the cliffs turn rose and amber. The area has a few acacia trees and tough shrubs, and the occasional herd of goats.

Practical advice here is sobering. Yemen's civil war has centered on Ma'rib for years, and the region has seen front-line fighting, mines and a large displaced population. Foreign travel advisories are firm in advising against visits, and nobody should plan a ride in this area without reliable and current information, which at present argues for staying home. The sites are best understood through books, museum collections and the work of archaeologists who documented them in calmer times.

In earlier years, travelers came by road from Sana'a, about a hundred and thirty kilometers away, over mountain passes and then desert tracks, and stayed in Ma'rib, where fuel and simple meals could be found. It remains one of the great ancient landscapes of the Arab world.
t.ancient dam of ma rib dam of aljufaynah@:
Not every part of the Ma'rib story belongs to the famous main dam. The Jufaynah dam, or Dam of al-Jufaynah, is one of the smaller works in the system that the Sabaeans built across the valleys of the region, and it shows that the irrigation of the oasis was not a single structure but a network. Many wadis flow into the plain here, and the people of ancient Saba learned to channel each of them, building diversion walls, canals and distribution boxes so that the flood could be shared among fields.

Less is written about this site than about the main dam, and it is better to be honest about that than to embroider. What can be said is that it belongs to the same Sabaean tradition of dressed stone and mud-brick works, that it sits within a few kilometers of Ma'rib, and that its purpose was to hold and direct floodwater to farmland. The care taken in the masonry and in the water control follows the same logic as the larger dam, and together the structures reveal a society that organized labor and law around water.

The landscape is arid and open, with low stony hills, dry watercourses and scattered date palms where the water still reaches. The ground is pale, the sky bright and the air hot, and after rare rain the wadis flood suddenly and brown water fills channels that have been dry for months. The line between flood and drought is sharp here, which is the reason the dams mattered.

Today the area is dangerous. Ma'rib has been a front line in Yemen's war since 2014, with fighting, mines and a heavy military presence around the city and the surrounding hills. Foreign governments advise against any travel, and a rider thinking of the roads here should wait until conditions are safe and information is reliable. It is not a place to improvise.

In peaceful times, the sites around Ma'rib were reached on a short drive from the town, which offered fuel, tea and simple meals. A local guide who knew the dams and the tracks between them was a valuable companion, and a hat and plenty of water were essential.
t.bar an temple@15.4,45.3:
Barran, or Bar'ān, is the smaller companion to the great temple of Awwam, and the local name for it is Arsh Bilqis, the Throne of Bilqis. It was another sanctuary of Almaqah, the moon god of the Sabaeans, and it stood at the edge of the oasis a few kilometers from Ma'rib, where its pillars rose above the dunes. What remains today is a wall of finely cut stone and a row of tall pillars standing in front of it, silhouetted against the pale sky.

The pillars are the most striking part. They are monolithic, square in section and capped with simple tops, and they once held up a roof over the entrance hall of the temple. Beyond them, a large court with benches and an altar for offerings lay open to the sky. The temple was used over many centuries, and inscriptions on the stones preserve the names of kings and the dates of repairs. The masonry is precise and tight, and the proportions give the ruin a quiet grace.

The temple is bound up with the tradition of the Queen of Sheba. Local people call it her throne, and the name has stuck, even though archaeologists tie the temple to the moon god rather than to a historical queen. Tradition and archaeology often sit side by side in this valley, and it is a pleasure to hear a guide move easily between them.

Any account of this place must deal with the present. Ma'rib governorate is in an area of conflict, and the surrounding region has seen shelling and displacement. International advice is against travel, and a visitor, especially a rider on an independent trip, should treat the area as closed unless trusted and current local information says otherwise. It is better to read, and to wait.

Before the war, visitors reached Barran by a short drive from Ma'rib, and found fuel, tea and basic meals in town. Sunrise and sunset were the best times, when the pillars glowed amber and the sand was cool. In the middle of the day, the heat was fierce, and a scarf and water were more important than a camera.
t.sviyazhsk@55.8,48.7:
Sviyazhsk is a small island town that looks as if it were floating on the Volga. It sits at the meeting of the Volga and the Sviyaga rivers in Tatarstan, and it was founded in 1551 by Ivan the Terrible as a military base for the campaign against the Khanate of Kazan. The wooden fortress was built far upstream, near Uglich, floated down the river in pieces on rafts and assembled on this hill in about four weeks, a feat of logistics that astonished contemporaries. A year later the tsar's army took Kazan, and the town became an outpost of Russian rule and Orthodox mission.

Its beauty today lies in the quiet cluster of old churches and monasteries on the hill. The Assumption Cathedral, built in the 1550s, has frescoes inside that include an unusual image of St. Christopher with the head of a dog, a rarity in Orthodox art, and a wall painting of a vast and detailed Last Judgment. The Monastery of St. John the Baptist and the Trinity church stand close by, and a small museum and craft workshops operate in some of the old buildings. The town was an island from the 1950s, when the Kuybyshev reservoir flooded the lowlands, and now a causeway connects it to the mainland. UNESCO added it to the World Heritage list in 2017.

The area is low, green and open, and the Volga is wide and slow, with willows and reeds along the shore. The road from Kazan, about forty kilometers to the east, is fast and smooth with moderate traffic, and the final approach across the causeway is a lovely moment, with water on both sides. Weekends in summer are busy with tourists, and the quietest hours are early morning or late afternoon. The wind from the water can be fresh, so bring a layer.

Services in the village are small. A few cafes and guesthouses operate in summer, but fuel and shops are better found in Vasilyevo, a short distance away, or in Kazan. The island has few cars and a walking pace.

Linger until the day-trippers have gone. In the evening light, the domes glow against the water, and the island is tranquil.
t.cochrane chile@-47.3,-72.6:
Cochrane is the last proper town on the southern Carretera Austral before the road runs out into the far south, and it feels like it. About three thousand people live here, in low houses around a spacious plaza, with a river valley and glacial lakes nearby and the high Patagonian steppe to the east. It was founded in the 1950s and named after Thomas Cochrane, the Scottish admiral who commanded the Chilean navy in the independence war against Spain, so there is an odd flavour of Scottish seafaring in the middle of the mountains.

The ride in from the north follows the shore of Lake General Carrera, the vast turquoise lake that Argentines call Buenos Aires Lake, and it is one of the most spectacular roads on the continent. The road clings to cliffs above the water, with sharp bends, gravel patches and sudden gusts of wind, while the lake changes colour from pale green to deep blue as the light moves. Past the lake, the road heads south along the Baker River, which carries more water than any other river in Chile, glowing a striking blue-green. Expect strong wind, quick weather changes and few other vehicles. Summer, from December to March, gives the longest days and the safest riding.

Cochrane is a practical stop. You will find fuel, a supermarket, simple restaurants serving lamb and local beer, and several guesthouses, and it is a good place to stock up for the Caleta Tortel road, which continues south and leads to a village built entirely on boardwalks over the water. Cochrane also serves as a gateway to Patagonia National Park, a huge reserve created from former sheep ranches, where guanacos, foxes and, with luck, pumas live.

The landscape is a blend of Andean peaks, glaciers and dry steppe. Rain falls heavily on the western side of the mountains, while the east is dry and windy, and Cochrane sits in a transition zone, with beech forest and grassland meeting. The air is clean and cold, and the night sky is a spectacle. The southern huemul deer also lives in the area, and condors are often seen soaring above the ridges.

Fill up the tank here, since the next fuel is a long way off. Bring warm layers, rain gear and patience, and watch the wind.
